Introduction: The Floor Plan on the Garage

The tape ran out before the room did.

I was on the garage floor with a roll of blue painter’s tape, marking the den in the patio home where Dad was supposed to move. I’d measured the real den the week before, standing in the empty unit with a tape measure and the leasing agent’s floor plan, writing numbers on the back of an envelope because I hadn’t thought to bring paper. Now I was laying those same numbers down in chalk-blue lines on concrete, because Dad kept asking how the furniture would “sit,” and a sheet with numbers on it didn’t answer that the way a room you could stand inside of did.

The measurements were close enough to make decisions. Earl’s recliner fit, with room to swing the footrest. The china cabinet did not. I’d known that before I unrolled the tape — I’d done the math twice — but knowing a thing on paper and showing a person the floor are not the same act of telling the truth.

Dad stood over the tape with his hands in his pockets. He looked at the outline of the cabinet, then at the recliner’s broad, familiar shape. He didn’t ask me to make the room bigger. He asked where the cabinet might go.

I didn’t have an answer yet. We stood there a while, looking at the lines. A neighbor’s sprinkler ticked on somewhere behind the garage. Dad didn’t say anything about Mom, and neither did I, but the cabinet had been hers — bought the first year they were married, moved four times in forty years, always against the same kind of wall. He wasn’t grieving a piece of furniture. He was doing arithmetic on what a life takes up, and finding out the new one held less than the old.

That was the move in miniature. A room had to work. A piece of furniture mattered for reasons that had nothing to do with its dimensions. There were feelings in the middle of both, and a decision still needed making, on a schedule that didn’t particularly care how anyone felt about it.

Downsizing a parent is a logistics problem wearing a grief costume. The phrase sounds tidy; the work rarely is. You may be measuring rooms while your parent is grieving the house — not just the house as a building, but the house as the last place that still held the version of their life where they could manage on their own. You may be trying to keep a dozen small deadlines — a lease signature, a mover’s deposit, a utility shutoff — from becoming one large emergency. Meanwhile, you may be fielding opinions from siblings who live elsewhere. They may feel entitled to a vote without doing any of the carrying. You may also notice your parent has started repeating the same question about the closing date, not because of memory trouble, but because asking it again is a way of making sure the ground is still there. You can love your parent and still get tired of being the person with the list. Both of those are true at once, and neither one cancels the other.

I know the list. I dispatched trucks for years. A load needed a driver, a destination, and a time it had to be there. If any one of those three things was missing, the load sat on the dock while everyone argued about whose fault that was. Family life is not freight, and a parent is not a delivery. A dock worker doesn’t flinch when a shipment gets delayed. A parent flinches when the moving truck is a week later than she told her garden club it would be. Now she has to explain the delay to people she’s known for thirty years, and the explaining feels like one more small failure stacked on a big one. But the useful part of dispatch still applies, stripped of everything else: a task without an owner and a date tends to sit until somebody is upset. That part of the job translates cleanly, even when nothing else about it does.

My two rules are plain. Give every task an owner and a drop date. And don’t use guilt as a planning tool. Guilt can tell you that you care; it cannot tell you which apartment fits, who is calling the mover, or when the house needs to be ready. I learned the second rule by breaking it. Early on, I caught myself telling a sibling that Dad “deserved better” than a slow callback on a question about the lease, as if speed were love and a delay were its absence. It wasn’t a useful sentence. It didn’t get the callback made any faster. It put my sibling on the defensive instead of on the phone, which is the opposite of what a callback needs. Guilt is loud, but it isn’t a tool. It doesn’t tighten a bolt or confirm a delivery window. A date on a calendar does both.

This book follows the order most families encounter the work. First comes the question of whether the current home still fits, and the harder question underneath it — who gets to decide that, and how you raise it without handing your parent an ultimatum disguised as a conversation.

Then you compare next-home options: a smaller house, a 55+ community, independent or assisted living, or moving in with family. Each option carries its own costs and trade-offs that no single number can capture for every reader, which is exactly why a later chapter builds a worksheet instead of quoting one figure and calling the question settled.

From there you sort what will move, decide what to sell or donate, and divide family keepsakes. Those are three different kinds of hard that get lumped together in most people’s heads as “going through the house.” They actually call for three different approaches, and often three different moods in the same room on the same afternoon — a calm, practical hour of sorting can turn, without warning, into an argument over who gets the mantel clock.

Later, you’ll work through choosing a mover without getting scammed, the mechanics and tax questions of the house sale. Moving day itself, setting up the new place for safety, and the weeks of settling in that follow each have their own chapter. Each piece has its own chapter. Trying to do everything at once leads to expensive decisions in a tired kitchen at ten at night.

The order is a guide, not a test. A parent may already have chosen a place before anyone else in the family has caught up to the idea that a move is happening at all. A lease may set the move date before the attic is sorted, which means the sorting chapter gets read out of order and in a hurry, and that’s fine — the tools inside it work just as well under pressure as they do with time to spare. A family may need to pause entirely, for a hospital stay, a holiday, or simply because everyone needs a week where nobody mentions the word “downsizing” at dinner. Start with the decision in front of you and use the later chapters when their work arrives. You do not have to read this as a race from page one to the moving truck, and treating it like one is a good way to miss the parts that would have saved you a fight three weeks later.

This is a book about ordinary moving logistics and family coordination, written for the adult child who has become the one holding the clipboard. It is not a dementia-care guide. If dementia-specific needs are central — changes in judgment, driving safety, or the grief of a diagnosis layered onto a move — see The Dementia Caregiver’s First Year.

This book also is not a legal or tax guide, and the line matters more than it sounds like it should. An adult child does not gain authority to sign a lease, hire movers, or sell a parent’s property just by taking charge of the calendar, however capable or well-meaning. Authority to act for someone else must come from a specific legal source. Most often that’s a power of attorney the parent signed while able to; in its absence, it may take a court-appointed guardianship instead. Without one of those in place, a signature on a lease or a closing document may not hold up, and finding that out partway through a move is far worse than finding it out now.

When authority or capacity is uncertain, pause before making commitments. Ask a licensed elder law attorney what the existing documents permit. Tax questions about a house sale are their own kind of specific. The rules depend on how long the home was owned, how it was used, and circumstances particular to your parent. They belong with a CPA or tax professional who can look at the actual numbers, not a chapter in a book that has never seen your parent’s closing statement.

You don’t need to turn into a project manager with a color-coded wall to do this well. A sheet of paper will do, at least at the start. Write down the next task, the person who owns it, and the date it needs to happen. If the task involves a decision rather than just an errand, write down who gets to make that decision, and say so out loud to the people it affects, before the decision gets made in a way that surprises somebody. That’s enough to start, and it’s more than most families have when this work begins. The family work plan gets its full treatment later, when the first chapter builds it out with the details a real move needs — who approves a purchase above a certain amount, where receipts get kept, when the family checks in with each other. For now, the two rules are enough: an owner, a date, and no guilt standing in for either one.

Dad’s recliner had a place in the den. The china cabinet needed another answer, and the answer did not have to come that afternoon, or even that week. For now, the tape on the floor gave us something useful: a room we could see, and one decision we could make without pretending it was the only one left to make, or the hardest one still coming.

Chapter 10: Deciding It’s Time

The daughter had left her coat on.

In this kitchen-table example, she had come to talk about the basement stairs, but she was standing beside the refrigerator with her car keys in her hand. Her mother was seated by the window, folding a grocery receipt into smaller and smaller squares.

“Your sister thinks we should start looking,” the daughter said.

“Looking at what?”

There it was. Having discussed a possible move with her sister before asking her mother what she wanted, the daughter now had a problem that went beyond the stairs.

She put down the keys. Took off the coat.

“I’ve gotten ahead of myself. Can we start with the laundry? You said you haven’t wanted to go downstairs since you slipped. I’d like to know what’s happening, and what you want to do about it.”

Her mother unfolded the receipt. “I want someone to move the washer. I didn’t say I wanted to move myself.”

That wasn’t agreement to downsize. It was information.

Ask before you arrange

Start with your parent as the decision-maker while they are able to make the decision. Not as the person you hope will ratify something the children settled last Sunday.

Ask permission to discuss the house, including what help your parent wants and what they want left alone; agreeing to this conversation doesn’t authorize a tour or a deposit.

The authority boundary from the introduction applies here: collecting information doesn’t entitle you to sign a lease, enter a moving contract for your parent, or authorize selling their property.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s explanation of power of attorney, reviewed in August 2026, warns about an agent doing things the person never authorized. Before a commitment, establish who will be bound by it and who has documented authority for that particular action, rather than assuming one document covers every job.

If capacity or authority is uncertain or disputed, stop commitments and property transfers and consult a licensed elder law attorney. A family vote cannot settle that question. Nor should you ask your parent to sign something they may not understand just to keep the calendar moving.

Rules differ by state. California Courts, for example, says needing help alone does not justify appointing a conservator; less restrictive options must be considered. That’s a California safeguard, not a set of instructions for your state. Use your own state court’s self-help information and have the attorney explain the documents and authority your particular situation requires.

A disagreement isn’t a capacity assessment. You can think a choice is unwise and still have no right to replace it with yours.

Look at an ordinary week

The house can be beautiful and no longer work. It can also look shabby and still suit the person living there. Neither the peeling porch paint nor your dislike of the upstairs bathroom decides the matter.

Look at what your parent must do to get through an ordinary week. Where do they sleep? Can they reach the bathroom they use? How do clean clothes get upstairs? Who brings food into the kitchen? What happens when the person who helps is away?

Don’t ask your parent to demonstrate a difficult staircase to prove they can manage it; ask about the task instead, without requiring a performance done for your benefit.

Separate what you saw from what you suspect. “The laundry basket was at the basement door on both visits” is an observation. “You can’t take care of yourself” is a verdict. Leave the verdict out of your notebook.

The National Institute on Aging, in “Aging in Place: Growing Older at Home,” recommends thinking about support before care needs become large and revisiting plans as needs change. Its guidance includes household help and transportation. That leaves room for an answer other than moving: the current house may work with support your parent wants and can arrange.

Use this checklist to identify subjects for discussion, not to count up a moving score. Beside each item, write an actual example, what your parent says about it, and whether workable help exists.

  • Essential rooms require stairs your parent reports finding difficult or has stopped using.
  • A fall or near fall has changed how your parent moves around the house.
  • Groceries, laundry or necessary repairs are not getting done, or depend on help that has no dependable arrangement.
  • Your parent wants company or outings but cannot arrange a way to reach them.
  • A spouse’s death has left household jobs without someone willing and able to do them.
  • Your parent says the house takes more work, money or attention than they want to give it.
  • The current arrangement depends on family help that the family cannot actually sustain.

A checked box means something needs attention, not that a move is the answer.

A fall also needs its own health-care conversation. NIA’s “Falls and Fractures in Older Adults” advises telling a doctor about a fall even when there was no pain, because a medical issue may be involved. Ask your parent to contact their clinician; don’t assume a new address will solve the cause. An immediate medical emergency belongs with emergency services, not a housing discussion.

After a spouse dies, the quiet house may be painful, comforting, or both; ask which parts of living there still matter and which jobs have become hard without the other person. Selling it is no promise of company.

If dementia-specific judgment, driving or safety concerns are central, use the dementia-caregiving companion in this series rather than treating this checklist as an assessment.

Your own workload belongs on the page too. If you’re doing the laundry every Saturday but those visits are about to become impossible, write that down and say so, even if nobody wants a move.

Give “not yet” a date

“You’ll break a hip and then you’ll have no choice” is a threat wearing a sensible coat. You cannot know that outcome. Explain the unresolved task instead.

Explain what waiting would leave unresolved. If the laundry isn’t getting done, that remains a problem next week. If the neighbor who brings groceries is leaving town, that help has an end date. A crisis can compress the time available to explore options; planning beforehand gives you something to work with if circumstances change.

“Not yet” can be a decision. It needs an accompanying plan for the present house and a date to review whether that plan works.

Your parent might want to investigate laundry help before considering a move. Agree who will ask and when you’ll discuss the answer; don’t turn that inquiry into a secret apartment search while your parent thinks you’re calling about the washing. If the help isn’t available or your parent doesn’t want it at the quoted price, return to the problem with that information.

The Administration for Community Living’s Eldercare Locator, at eldercare.acl.gov, can help you find local service contacts, including an Area Agency on Aging. Ask what exists in your parent’s area; don’t build a staying-home plan around a service whose availability and terms nobody has checked.

Your limits need dates too. “I can bring groceries through the end of this month, but I can’t continue after that” is a boundary. “Move or you’ll never see me again” is an ultimatum. The first identifies a task needing replacement. The second makes the relationship the price of agreement.

An unresolved decision stays unresolved; it doesn’t become yours because you are tired. Offer an appropriate professional conversation and be honest about what you can provide.

Keep the first table small

Ask your parent whom they want in the first conversation. That may be you alone, both parents, another child, or a trusted person who helps them speak freely. Don’t gather every sibling around the table and call it support if your parent experiences it as a hearing.

When both parents are involved, ask each for their view rather than making the more talkative one the spokesperson; one may be ready to leave while the other is not.

Choose a quiet time your parent agrees to, with enough privacy to discuss the house without an audience. Put away the phone. Ask whether hearing, printed information or a different meeting time would make the conversation easier.

Leave the real estate agent and the eager relative with a pickup out of this first talk. A sales appointment is not a neutral opening for a parent who hasn’t agreed to explore moving.

If a sibling joins remotely, agree that one person will speak at a time. Discuss family workload separately, without bargaining over your parent’s home in front of them.

Don’t promise that everyone will get a vote. Ask your parent what information may be shared, with whom, and how. Helping with errands does not entitle each helper to every financial detail.

A page to take into the conversation

Write your own version of this script on one page, using words you can say without sounding as though you’ve been sent by a committee. Leave space for the answers.

Ask permission. “I’d like to talk about how the house is working for you. Is this a good time? We don’t need to decide about a move today.”

Name one observation. “You told me you’ve stopped carrying the washing downstairs. I want to understand what you’re doing instead and whether you want help.”

Ask what matters. “What would you miss most if you left? What would you be glad not to do anymore?” Let the answers stand. Don’t counter every attachment with an amenity brochure.

Offer a limited next step. “Would you like me to find out about help with that job? Or would you rather we begin looking at what a different place could offer? I won’t arrange either without your agreement.”

Close with permission and a date. “What are you comfortable with me doing before we talk again? Who may I update? Let’s choose when we’ll sit down with the answer.”

If your parent says, “You’re trying to get rid of my house,” answer the concern, not the accusation. “I haven’t arranged a sale. I am worried about the stairs, and I’d like to discuss what would help.” Only say that if it is true.

If you already made calls without asking, own it. “I got ahead of you. I should have asked first.” Don’t defend the calls for ten minutes and then ask for trust.

If the answer is no, stop the pitch. You can seek general guidance about your concerns without claiming consent your parent hasn’t given, but don’t keep negotiating until they give in.

What helped with Dad was asking what he wanted me to do next, then waiting for his answer. Even after the garage-floor measuring, I still had to listen.

Put the work on paper

Once your parent agrees to a next step, build the family work plan promised in the introduction; this sheet follows the move through later chapters as new jobs appear.

Use one sheet your parent can read, with one person keeping the current version. Copy the header once and the ten-field row for each agreed task.

Sheet permission and status: [What your parent agreed to explore; what is not decided; actions not authorized]

Weekly update: [Day and method; who may receive the update; next check-in]

Blank task row:

  • Task and limit: [result; what not to arrange]
  • Owner: [name]
  • Due date: [date]
  • Decision-maker: [name]
  • Contracting party and signer: [name or none; authority confirmed or unresolved]
  • Spending limit: [$ amount]
  • Approver: [who approves an expense or excess]
  • Payer and reimbursement: [who pays; whether reimbursement is authorized]
  • Quotes and receipts: [agreed location]
  • Status and update: [permission status; date and next step]

Completed laundry inquiry example:

  • Task and limit: Call local providers for availability and written prices; do not book service.
  • Owner: Daughter.
  • Due date: Tuesday.
  • Decision-maker: Parent.
  • Contracting party and signer: None; no signing authority needed for this inquiry.
  • Spending limit: $0.
  • Approver: Parent before any expense.
  • Payer and reimbursement: None authorized.
  • Quotes and receipts: Agreed folder.
  • Status and update: Information only; no contract or spending. Report at Sunday’s update.

The owner does the work; the decision-maker chooses. Gathering a quote doesn’t authorize accepting it. This plan grants no legal authority; the authority gate above still applies before anyone commits your parent to a contract or property transfer.

Give remote siblings specific jobs, such as finding service contacts or keeping this sheet current, with your parent’s permission. Ask each helper to accept the task and date rather than writing “help when needed.”

At the weekly update, report completed work, blocked tasks and decisions awaiting your parent’s answer. Replace missed dates or unavailable owners. Share only agreed information and any required reporting; keep identity documents and sensitive financial records out of an open family thread.

When your parent agrees to compare possible homes, use the worksheet in Chapter 11. For now, put only the action permitted today on this sheet.

Before you leave the kitchen, read that action back to your parent. Write down who has it and the date you’ll return with an answer. Leave them a copy they can find without asking you.

Chapter 11: Choosing the Next Home

“Who comes if I need help getting to the bathroom at night?” the father asked the sales representative.

“We have a wonderful emergency response system.”

His daughter wrote “night help — who, and what help?” beside the apartment number. The brochure stayed closed on her lap. Beyond the representative, the dining-room tables had cloth napkins and little vases of flowers.

This is an illustrative tour, but the missing detail is one to ask about yourself. “Who answers it, and what help can that person provide?” she asked.

A button could summon someone without that person providing the help her father meant. They needed the actual arrangement in writing.

The napkins were nice. They weren’t the service he was asking about.

Match the address to the help

Use the home-fit observations from Chapter 10 to describe what the next place must do. Not “somewhere safer” or “a place with people.” Write the job: meals without daily cooking, transportation to appointments, or help with a particular personal task.

Ask your parent what would make an ordinary day pleasant there: a working kitchen may matter more than organized outings, and nearby friends may matter more than being close to the children.

Their day. Their preferences.

If you don’t know what personal assistance your parent needs, ask their clinician before narrowing the search. If you cannot tell what support is necessary, pause the housing search and ask the clinician who knows your parent to identify the help the next setting must reliably provide. A sales representative’s reassurance isn’t a clinical assessment.

Read each property’s service description and agreement; these categories aren’t promises.

A smaller house or apartment

A smaller ordinary home lets your parent choose a different layout without buying a care package, but fewer rooms don’t arrange meals or transportation, even if the kitchen is easier to reach.

A landlord may handle building repairs; that doesn’t tell you who changes the sheets or brings in groceries.

Price the housing and the needed help separately. For an owned home, collect property-tax and insurance information, association charges if applicable, and a realistic maintenance allowance. For a rental, get the rent and required fees in writing. Add utilities and services that aren’t included.

Don’t enter “daughter will help” where a paid service quote belongs unless you have agreed to that particular job.

A community advertised as 55+

Treat “55+” as a reason to ask about residency requirements, not evidence that anyone provides personal care. Ask for the community’s eligibility and occupancy rules, along with its service list.

Find out exactly what association dues or other community charges cover. Lawn maintenance is one job. Housekeeping is another.

A clubhouse can be available while your parent still needs to arrange every trip beyond the gate, including the grocery run that nobody mentioned while admiring the pool on the tour.

Ask about visiting grandchildren, pets, parking, or a relative staying to help. Get the governing documents and compare household costs, not just the advertised housing payment.

Independent living

For a place advertised as independent living, ask which household jobs the fee buys. You may be offered meals, housekeeping, transportation or activities; put each inclusion on the sheet, with its limits.

“Transportation included” needs destinations, booking arrangements and operating hours before it becomes useful information, especially if your parent’s appointment is across town before breakfast and the bus doesn’t leave until later.

Don’t infer hands-on personal care from the word “senior,” an emergency pendant, or staff being somewhere in the building. Ask whether care is provided, who provides it, and whether an outside provider is permitted if your parent needs one.

Investigate this option if your parent wants less household work and opportunities for company. If care must be purchased separately, its price and availability belong beside the housing quote.

Assisted living

The National Institute on Aging describes assisted living as housing for people who need help with daily care, but not the degree of help a nursing home provides. Its guidance names personal care, medication help and household services while emphasizing that arrangements vary by facility and state.

Take specific needs to the staff member responsible for assessing care, not just the person giving the tour. Ask what the facility can provide now, what it cannot provide, and how that determination affects admission and price.

A care tier is the provider’s category for a package or level of assistance; the name alone doesn’t tell you which tasks it includes or which particular help costs extra.

Ask what triggers reassessment, who makes it, and how a change affects the bill. Also ask what happens if your parent’s needs exceed what the facility can support.

If a campus offers independent living, assisted living and nursing care, get the terms for each transition. Don’t assume an available apartment today reserves a future care bed or fixes its price.

Moving in with family

Your spare bedroom is a housing option. It isn’t a care arrangement until the necessary help has been agreed and made workable.

Talk with everyone who lives there before treating the room as available. Discuss privacy, bathroom access and ordinary household routines with your parent. Can they close a door and have company without asking permission? Where will their mail go? Who can be home when help is needed?

Write down additional household costs, any agreed contribution, and quotes for outside help. Put planned work changes beside those costs so nobody mistakes reduced earnings for spare time. A family estimate is not a provider quote; label it honestly.

Arrange backup for any essential help a family member agrees to give, and decide when to review the arrangement; wanting your parent nearby doesn’t make an uncovered weekday disappear from the calendar.

A national price isn’t your quote

CareScout’s Cost of Care Survey reports a 2025 national median assisted-living cost of $6,200 a month, or $74,400 a year. The survey was conducted from July through November 2025. These are the survey’s 2025 figures, not a promise of a 2026 price in your town.

CareScout cautions that an individual provider’s cost can differ considerably from the median and that setting, services and support affect cost. The median isn’t a minimum or maximum.

I wouldn’t choose a home from that number. Start the budget conversation there, then obtain written local quotes.

Give each provider the same description of your parent’s needs, with their permission, and request an itemized quote dated for the proposed unit and the services you actually discussed on the visit.

Not a “starting at” advertisement.

Keep recurring costs separate from money needed before occupancy. A community fee, entrance fee or deposit can have different payment and refund terms; record the provider’s actual terms rather than treating the names as interchangeable. Ask what happens to each payment if admission doesn’t proceed.

For monthly charges, identify what is included in the base rent, what belongs to the care tier, and what is charged separately. Don’t add a medication or laundry charge twice if it is already included. Don’t mark an unknown price as zero because nobody has answered yet.

Ask how rates can change and how long the written quote remains valid. If the price depends on an assessment that hasn’t happened, label it provisional. Keep the unanswered charge visible until the provider supplies an answer.

Keep Medicare out of the rent column

Medicare.gov’s “Long-term care” coverage page says Medicare does not pay for ongoing nonmedical, custodial long-term care. That includes help with basic personal tasks such as bathing, dressing and using the bathroom. Moving into assisted living doesn’t turn those services into a Medicare benefit.

Covered medical services are a separate matter. Medicare’s rules for skilled nursing facility care are different from ongoing custodial care; don’t use a relative’s covered rehabilitation stay as evidence that your parent’s housing and daily assistance will be paid for.

Ask the plan or insurer about the particular service, not whether it “covers this place.” Confirm benefit terms before counting that money. Medicare.gov also says Medigap doesn’t pay for long-term care services.

If your parent has long-term care insurance, ask the insurer to confirm whether this setting and the proposed services meet the policy’s conditions. Medicaid eligibility and covered services depend on state rules and the person’s circumstances; ask the state Medicaid agency rather than assuming approval from a facility’s brochure.

Before a substantial financial commitment, have an elder law attorney review unclear admission, exit, refund or personal-payment clauses. You need to know whether a child’s signature would create a personal payment obligation, not merely where to put the initials. A CPA or qualified tax professional can help your parent assess a funding plan with tax consequences. Neither job belongs to the sales desk.

Tour the day your parent would live

The National Institute on Aging’s facility-selection guide recommends visiting different facilities, asking about staffing and costs, and returning at another time, including mealtime. Use that approach without turning the tour into an inspection you aren’t qualified to perform.

Let your parent address the staff. Notice whether the reply comes back to them or passes straight over their head to you.

Ask to see the proposed unit rather than just a decorated model, and walk the routes your parent expects to use without asking them to prove they can manage a difficult task.

Take these questions into a service-based community:

  • Which meals and household services are included, and what limits or extra charges apply?
  • Who provides the personal help we described, including at night and on weekends? What happens when someone requests help?
  • What transportation is offered, how is it booked, and what trips cost extra?
  • Who assesses care needs, what changes the care charge, and what needs cannot be supported here?
  • What activities actually take place during the week and on weekends? May my parent try one before deciding?
  • What are the admission, waitlist, deposit, cancellation and move-out terms? Can we take the agreement home to review?

For night-time help, ask what responding staff are trained and authorized to do. Keep an unanswered care question open; don’t fill it with your best guess.

Licensing categories and oversight differ by state. In North Carolina, for example, the Department of Health and Human Services’ Adult Care Licensure Section provides adult care facility information and links to inspections, ratings and penalties. Use its official site for that state. Elsewhere, ask your state health or human services department which agency oversees this type of setting and how to obtain the relevant records.

Match records to the actual facility and care setting, not just the company’s name. Read any cited problem and ask what action followed; a favorable record doesn’t answer whether this particular unit and service package provide the help your parent needs at night.

Put every option on the same sheet

Use facing pages or separate sheets laid beside one another. Copy the same fields for each serious option, including a family home. You’re comparing complete arrangements, not competing rents.

Write the needs and preferences being measured, then copy this worksheet for each address:

  • Option and unit: [address; housing type; proposed unit]
  • Quote record: [provider/contact; written quote date; valid through; final or provisional]
  • Base housing: [monthly rent/payment; services already included]
  • Care tier: [monthly amount; assistance included; assessment still needed]
  • Care add-ons: [each separate service and price; not counted in the tier]
  • Other recurring costs: [utilities, meals, transport, dues, taxes, insurance, maintenance or outside help as applicable; frequency]
  • Monthly comparison total: [known recurring costs converted to monthly amounts; list every unpriced item separately]
  • Upfront charges: [community/entrance fees, deposits or housing purchase funds; due dates; written refund terms]
  • Service fit: [each essential need; who provides it; hours and limits; any uncovered need]
  • Parent’s preferences: [what suits them; what they would give up]
  • Distance: [travel time from key family or friends; transport for the parent’s usual destinations]
  • Availability: [unit available or waitlist; conditions; deposit terms; estimated date and who supplied it]
  • Change and exit terms: [rate increases; care reassessment; needs requiring another setting; notice/refund terms]
  • Open questions: [missing price, service confirmation, record or contract review]

For an ordinary home, mark the care tier “not applicable” and enter outside help separately. For a family home, use agreed household estimates and written outside-service quotes. Include only costs attributable to this arrangement.

If a quote includes laundry and another excludes it, obtain the second laundry price before comparing totals. If a yearly charge is converted to a monthly allowance, retain the original amount and frequency beside it. Your parent needs to know when the money actually leaves the account.

Keep purchase funds and refundable deposits separate from recurring charges. They still matter to affordability. A total with missing charges is incomplete, however attractive it looks.

Record travel time honestly. Try the trip when you expect to make it, rather than using the mileage to promise visits you can’t sustain once the road fills up with people going home from work.

Check affordability in private

After completing the option sheets, make a separate affordability check with your parent. They control who sees it. A lower price does not establish that they can pay it.

Start with confirmed monthly funds they are willing and able to use for housing and help, after allowing for their other expenses. Keep confidential balances and account details off shared family records.

Copy these fields onto the private sheet:

  • Parent’s monthly funds: [confirmed amount available for this arrangement; what your parent agrees to use]
  • Contributions or insurance: [each confirmed amount; payer; payment dates; conditions and duration; unconfirmed amounts marked unknown, not counted as available]
  • Confirmed monthly funding total: [parent’s available amount plus confirmed contributions or insurance; no double counting]
  • Each option’s monthly cost and gap: [option; known monthly cost; unpriced items; cost minus confirmed funding; a positive result is a shortfall]
  • Upfront funding: [each option’s charges and due dates; confirmed funds your parent agrees to use; when available; any shortfall or unresolved condition]
  • Parent’s agreed affordability status: [funding confirmed for quoted costs, not affordable on confirmed funds, or undecided; date checked]

Keep upfront funds separate from monthly funding. Don’t count the same money as both a deposit payment and an ongoing source without showing what remains. An insurance payment awaiting approval is unknown, even if someone expects approval soon.

If a gap, missing price or funding condition remains unresolved, keep the option undecided. Take complex funding or tax questions to the elder law attorney or qualified tax professional already named before making a commitment. Share only the agreed affordability status, not the private figures.

Leave with the missing answer

An option with an essential need uncovered is not ready for selection, even if its known monthly total is lowest. Resolve that gap before ranking the remaining places by cost and your parent’s preferences. A waitlist estimate needs an interim arrangement, not a move date built on hope.

Record the agreed task on the Chapter 10 work plan.

Take the completed sheets back to your parent. Ask which place they want to revisit and which answer they need before they could choose.

For the father with the unopened brochure, it was the night-time help. Write that question at the top of the page. Come home with the name of the person who can answer it.

Chapter 12: Sorting a Lifetime of Belongings

There were fourteen keys in the drawer by Dad’s back door, and not one of them opened anything he still owned.

I know, because I tried them. On a Saturday. For most of an hour, while two unlabeled boxes sat behind me and the kitchen cabinets stayed shut.

That hour taught me the only rule of sorting I’d defend to a stranger: the question is never “what is this?” The question is “where does this go, and who decides that.” I’d have spent the whole day on keys otherwise, and felt busy, and moved nothing.

So before anybody opens a drawer, the family needs a system. Not a mood. A mood puts you on the floor with a shoebox of photographs at four in the afternoon, crying over a cousin’s wedding, with the linen closet still full.

Start with the space, not the stuff

What fits is a measurement, not an opinion, and it belongs to the new place rather than the old one.

Get the actual dimensions of the next home, and get them written down: each room’s length and width, the ceiling height if anything tall is in question, the width of the doorways and any turn in a hallway. Count the storage, because that number is the one that surprises people. How many closets, how deep, with how many shelves. How many kitchen cabinets. Whether there is a linen closet, a coat closet, an attic, a basement, a garage, or none of those.

Ask the leasing office or the seller for a floor plan with measurements on it, and check it against the real room if you can get inside. A plan drawn to sell an apartment is not a tape measure.

Dad’s den was already laid out in blue tape on my garage floor by the time we started on the house, so we weren’t guessing about the recliner.

Then do the arithmetic in the direction nobody likes. Furniture first, because furniture decides the floor. Measure each piece your parent wants to take, not the piece you assume they want. Put the pieces on the plan. When the plan fills up, it is full, and no amount of good intentions adds a wall.

Storage next. A parent who had three closets and now has one cannot keep three closets of clothes, and the honest way to say that is as a number, early, before forty hangers become an argument on moving day. Decide with your parent how much of the one closet goes to coats, how much to shoes, how much to the clothes they wear in a normal week.

Some things have no slot at all, and it’s kinder to say so plainly than to discover it with a truck at the curb. A chest freezer needs a place to plug in. A workshop bench needs a workshop. A dining set for ten needs a dining room, and many apartments give you a corner.

Where your parent is buying or renting an ordinary house instead, the same count applies. Fewer rooms is still fewer rooms.

Four buckets, and a box for the arguments

Every item gets exactly one of four destinations, named out loud when you put it down:

  • Goes: it moves to the new place and has a spot there.
  • Family: someone in the family has asked for it, and it waits for the dividing method in Chapter 14 rather than disappearing into a trunk this afternoon.
  • Sell or donate: it leaves the house through a sale or a donation, which Chapter 13 handles in detail, including the calls you make before you load anything.
  • Out: trash, recycling, or the special handling the next section covers.

Four is the whole list. The bucket I’d add if I were allowed a fifth isn’t a bucket at all; it’s one labeled box for the items your parent cannot decide about today.

That box needs two things written on the lid: the date, and the date you’ll open it again. An owner for it, too, if the box is going to live at your house for a while. Undecided is a legitimate answer. Undecided with no date is how a garage fills up for nine years.

Keep the box small on purpose. One box, not a room. If it fills, that’s information: the sessions are moving too fast for your parent, or you’re sorting the wrong room first.

Your parent names the destination, item by item, for as long as they’re able and willing to. You carry things. That division of labor is the whole job, and the consent and authority limits from Chapter 10 don’t loosen because you’re tired and standing in a hot attic. A daughter deciding that the good dishes are “obviously” going to Goodwill is making a decision that wasn’t hers.

When your parent says they want to keep something that doesn’t fit, write it on the undecided list instead of arguing in the moment. You already know what the plan says. Let the measurements do the disagreeing.

Label as you go, with a marker, on the box, on the side and not the top, because boxes get stacked. A sorted houseful in unmarked boxes is an unsorted houseful with extra steps.

And sort into containers you can actually move. Thirty pounds of books in a big box is a box that stays where it is until somebody’s back gives out.

Things that don’t go in a box

Three categories need their own handling, and all three turn up in the first week.

Medicines. You’ll find expired prescriptions, a half-bottle of something from a hospital stay, and pills in a drawer with no label at all. The Food and Drug Administration’s guidance on disposing of unused medicines says a take-back option is the best way to get rid of most unused or expired medicines, prescription and over-the-counter alike. That means a drug take-back location, or a prepaid drug mail-back envelope.

The FDA says authorized take-back locations in your community may include retail, hospital or clinic pharmacies and law enforcement facilities, some with kiosks or drop boxes. It also notes that the Drug Enforcement Administration periodically runs National Prescription Drug Take Back events.

Scratch out the personal information on pill bottle labels and packaging before you drop anything off; the FDA says to, and there’s a second reason. A parent’s name, address and prescription history on a label in a curbside bin is a gift to the wrong person.

If no take-back option is available, the FDA directs you to check its flush list. That list covers certain medicines the agency says to flush immediately when take-back isn’t at hand. For anything not on it, the FDA has separate instructions for the household trash. Read the agency’s own pages for the item in your hand rather than my paraphrase; guidance differs by medicine, and some products in unusual forms carry their own instructions.

What you do not do is sort your parent’s current medicines. Anything they’re taking now stays with them and travels with them, in its own labeled bag, not in the moving truck. If you aren’t sure whether a bottle is current, ask your parent, then ask their pharmacist. A pharmacist will answer a disposal question on the phone. Nobody in this book, including me, should be deciding what your parent keeps taking.

The garage shelf. Old paint, thinner, motor oil, pesticide, pool chemicals, drain cleaner, car batteries. The Environmental Protection Agency’s page on household hazardous waste, last updated in June 2026, says products such as paints, cleaners, oils, batteries and pesticides can contain hazardous ingredients and need special care at disposal. Many communities run collection programs for them.

Because household hazardous waste is regulated at the state and local level, the EPA tells you to contact your local environmental, health or solid waste agency about permanent or periodic collections near you. It also says to keep these products in their original containers and never to mix them. For a container that’s corroding, it says to call your local hazardous materials official or fire department.

Translated into your Saturday: the garage gets its own trip, to a place you phoned first, and nothing from that shelf rides in a box with linens.

Paper. Deeds, vehicle titles, insurance policies, tax records, military discharge papers, birth and marriage certificates, Social Security cards, bank and retirement statements. None of that gets sorted by volunteers and none of it goes out in a bag. Put every document of that kind in one container that your parent controls, and let them decide what stays, with their attorney or tax professional answering the questions about what can go. I’d rather you move a box of paper you later discover was unnecessary than shred a deed on a hot afternoon because the pile was tall.

Keep that container with your parent, or in the agreed place your family already uses for records, and keep it off any open family thread or shared photo album.

The items that aren’t about the item

Some objects are load-bearing. The piece looks like a cabinet and functions like a marriage.

You will know these when you meet them, because the conversation changes temperature. A parent who has been decisive for two hours goes quiet over a cake pan. That isn’t stubbornness, and it isn’t confusion. It’s a person weighing how much smaller the next life is allowed to be.

Don’t negotiate with it. Three things help more:

Let the item wait. Put it in the dated undecided box and say so out loud. Most people can decide about an object next week that they cannot decide about with a stranger’s truck in the driveway.

Offer the part instead of the whole. One teacup rather than the set of twelve. Two of the forty Christmas ornaments, in a labeled box, to be unpacked first at the new place. The serving platter that actually appears at Thanksgiving, not the full cabinet that mostly held dust.

Ask what the object is for. Not as a trick to talk them out of it. Ask because the answer sometimes names a need you can meet another way, and sometimes names a need only that object meets, in which case it goes and something else leaves instead.

Photographs deserve their own warning. Don’t sort photographs during a move. A shoebox of loose pictures will take four hours and produce one decision, and it will do that on the day you planned to finish the kitchen. Boxes of photographs go in the “goes” pile, intact, to be gone through later in a chair with coffee, which is the right way to go through them anyway. Same for letters, slides and home movies.

And if your parent asks you to take something you don’t want, think before you answer fast. “I’d be glad to have the quilt” is a sentence you should only say if it’s true. A thing passed along out of guilt gets resented in a basement for years. You can say, kindly, that you’d rather it went to someone who’d use it, and then help find that person.

Sort by the clock, not by the room

A houseful does not come apart in a weekend. Families try, usually because somebody flew in, and the result is a Sunday night with eleven unmarked boxes, two ruined tempers, and a parent who has stopped answering questions.

Work in sessions with a start time and a stop time, two or three hours, and stop when the clock says so even if the room isn’t finished. Put sessions on the family work plan from Chapter 10 the same way you put any other task there, with an owner and a date, so a sibling who intends to help has something specific to accept.

Order the rooms by stakes, lowest first. The linen closet, the garage shelving, the kitchen’s duplicate gadgets, the bathroom cabinet. Nobody’s heart lives in a stack of mismatched towels, and your parent gets to practice the system on easy things before it reaches the bedroom closet and the hutch.

Work in one room at a time, finished and labeled, before the next one opens. A house with six half-sorted rooms feels like no progress has been made, because it hasn’t.

Watch your parent’s energy rather than your schedule. Late afternoon is often a bad time for a long sorting session; so is the day after a medical appointment. Reschedule without making a speech about it. Two good hours beat five bad ones, and a parent who gets pushed through a bad session often takes the next one off entirely.

Take the “out” bags and the sell-or-donate boxes out of the house at the end of each session, or at least out of the room. Leaving them stacked in the hall invites second thoughts for two weeks and makes the place feel like a disaster instead of a plan.

One sheet per room

Write one of these before each room and keep it where the family can see it. Copy the header once, then the item lines as you need them.

  • Room and session: [room; date; start and stop time; who is sorting]
  • Space it must fit: [the room or storage it’s going to in the new place; measurements or shelf count]
  • Furniture decisions: [each piece; measurements; goes, family, sell or donate, or out]
  • Boxes packed: [how many; labeled with room and contents; where they’re stacked]
  • Family bucket: [each item someone has asked for; who asked; awaiting the Chapter 14 method]
  • Sell or donate: [what’s leaving this way; where it’s staged; whose task it is in Chapter 13]
  • Special handling: [medicines; hazardous items; documents; who is taking each one where]
  • Undecided box: [items in it; date boxed; date to reopen; who holds the box]
  • Not finished: [what’s left in this room; next session date and owner]

For a room your parent doesn’t want you in yet, fill out the first two lines and leave the rest blank. That’s a real status, and it belongs on the sheet instead of in your head.

The line that saves you is “not finished.” It converts a vague Sunday feeling into a date and a name, which is the only form in which the rest of the house actually gets sorted.

A kitchen sheet with something on it

Take an ordinary kitchen cupboard as a worked example. Your parent still cooks in this house, and the cupboard holds mixing bowls, measuring cups and baking tins. The new kitchen has one shelf available for those pieces. Today’s session covers that cupboard, not every kitchen decision you can think of while the door is open.

On the room sheet, write “lower cupboard beside oven” and the agreed session window. Under space, put the measured shelf width and depth from the new kitchen. Leave the furniture line blank. A blank that means “not applicable” is better than inventing work to fill a form.

Bring the shelf-sized outline to the table, on paper or marked with tape. Let your parent put the pieces they want inside it. The bowls can nest, but check the actual stack rather than assuming it will. Don’t win another inch by promising a high shelf your parent hasn’t agreed to use. The space allowance is a limit, not a test of how cleverly you can cram things in.

Suppose your parent chooses two bowls, one set of measuring cups and a baking tin. Write those names under boxes packed, but mark them “selected, still in use; not packed.” No carton has been closed. That distinction matters when another helper reads the sheet and assumes the cupboard is ready to empty.

Your parent wants a second tin to wait until the next session. Put its description and reopen date on the undecided line. That is the sentimental decision for today; you don’t have to explain the feeling or bargain over it. The worn duplicate bowls your parent approves releasing go under sell or donate, with destination still unconfirmed. Chapter 13 supplies the route. Nothing goes into a visitor’s bag because it happens to be beside the door.

Finish by recording exactly what remains: “chosen pieces still needed here; second tin undecided; upper cupboard untouched.” The next session begins from that sentence, not from a helper’s memory that the kitchen was nearly done. If your parent changes a choice, correct the old entry so two versions don’t survive.

Before leaving, restore the working cupboard with your parent. Keep today’s cooking pieces reachable and remove the empty cartons from the work area. Sorting should not leave them unable to make supper in the house they still live in. Ask them to show you what they’ll use tonight; don’t make another choice for them while tidying.

At the next visit, read that one sheet before opening anything else. You can continue the same cupboard or agree to change the pace. An unfinished room with an accurate record is more useful than a room declared finished because everyone wanted to go home.

Pick the easiest room in your parent’s house. Put two hours on the calendar with their agreement, and write down who’s bringing the marker and the boxes.

Then leave the keys in the drawer. The keys aren’t the job.

Chapter 13: Selling or Donating What Doesn’t Go

We backed a truck up to a thrift-store donation door with a load of encyclopedias and a sleeper sofa. The person at the door took one look and said they couldn’t accept either.

We had not called first. We had spent time loading, driven across town, and still had the same furniture. I remember the heat coming off the pavement and the quiet ride home. A donation is not a place you can assume will take whatever arrives.

Call before you haul. Every time.

A price tag is not a resale price

The china set bought for a wedding and the sofa bought for a small fortune both carry history. A buyer sees the item’s condition, size, and effort to collect it. What it cost years ago doesn’t tell you today’s price.

That can sting. It can also save you from spending three Saturdays trying to recover a price that exists only in the family’s memory.

Resale gets more promising when an item is clean, complete, working and easy to collect. A sturdy table with clear dimensions and a photograph may draw interest; a scratched table that needs a truck, two helpers and a narrow stairwell may not. The buyer’s labor counts, even if it doesn’t appear on your price label.

Don’t assume a set is worth more just because it is a set, or an object valuable because it looks old. If something seems unusually valuable, or several people disagree about its value, pause before selling it in a general lot. A qualified appraiser or specialist can help; an estimate is not an offer to buy, and the buyer should not be the only person telling you what it’s worth.

For ordinary household items, ask a simpler question: after the fee, the messages, the pickup and the time you spend, is selling still worth doing? A low price can be perfectly sensible if it gets a useful item to someone who wants it. It is not sensible if it turns into a part-time job the family resents.

What deserves a separate listing

Start with a small sample, not a whole room. Pick a few items your parent is comfortable offering, take clear photographs, and write down the work each one requires: measurements, cleaning, checking that it works, answering questions, arranging pickup. That gives you a real sense of the labor before you promise to list every lamp and side table.

Online asking prices can be tempting evidence, but an asking price only tells you what someone hopes to receive. It doesn’t show whether the item sold, what condition it was in, or what the buyer paid to collect it. If you look at listings, compare similar items in similar condition and use them as a rough point of reference, not an appraisal. Don’t spend money on repairs or professional cleaning just to chase an uncertain price without the owner’s agreement.

A bundle can save work when pieces belong together and the buyer can use them together. It can also narrow the group of people interested. Describe exactly what’s included and photograph the whole bundle; don’t hide a cracked plate or missing part in a broad phrase like “as-is.” For a lone item, honest dimensions and a plain description often prevent a long exchange with someone who discovers at the door that it won’t fit in their car.

Before listing, decide what happens if the item receives no suitable offer by the review date. The parent might lower the price, try consignment, or choose donation or removal instead. Write down that decision rule first. The listing is a trial, not permission to keep pursuing a sale after the owner has changed their mind.

Pick the route before moving the item

One-at-a-time sales take photographs, descriptions, messages and a pickup plan. They can suit a distinct item with a clear buyer, especially if the parent wants to be involved. Agree who answers inquiries and what offer needs approval. Don’t post an address or promise a pickup window before the household agrees.

Before an online listing

Keep the parent and any private papers out of the photographs. Use the platform’s own seller protections rather than arranging payment outside the app or account. Prefer a public local exchange when the item can move safely that way. Never share a verification code with a buyer, for any reason. Reject an overpayment and any request to refund the difference; a check clearing or funds appearing available does not mean the payment is good. Confirm payment inside the actual app or account before handing anything over, not from an email or a screenshot. Give out the home address only after the household has approved the buyer and the pickup. For a bulky item that has to be collected in person, have two adults present. See the FTC’s guidance on avoiding scams when selling online.

An estate-sale company may sell a larger collection at the home. Services, fees and handling of unsold property differ. Ask what’s included in setup, pricing, advertising, staffing and cleanup; how commission and extra charges work; when proceeds arrive; and what happens to leftovers. Get written terms before signing.

Consignment is narrower: a shop selects items, displays them, then pays the owner under an agreed arrangement if they sell. Ask what it will accept, how long it keeps each item, how its share is calculated, when payment is made, and what happens at the end of the term or if an item is damaged. Keep the pieces at home until the shop provides written terms.

A yard sale puts the family in charge of setup, pricing, questions, payment and leftovers. It may suit a modest number of inexpensive things if your parent likes the idea and someone has time. For a tired family, it may be the wrong job. Decide when it ends and where leftovers go before putting up a sign.

None of these routes promises a sale. A company may decline the collection, a shop may accept only select pieces, and yard-sale visitors may pass what you expected to sell. Choose an exit route for leftovers before a buyer is waiting at the door.

Choose a route for each item or group

Don’t assign one destination to the whole house. A good dining table, usable sheets and a broken recliner are separate decisions. The owner may approve one route for the table and another for the sheets. An unsold item needs a new decision; it is not permission to send the rest of the room away.

Start with a stop sign. If ownership is unclear, your parent hasn’t decided, or the person arranging the transfer lacks authority, don’t list, promise, donate or remove the item. If it belongs to the categories Chapter 12 set aside for special handling, take that route instead of putting it through an ordinary sale or cleanout. The rest of this decision path is for ordinary household property with a clear owner and an approved destination.

Next ask whether the item is a plausible sale candidate, not whether it once cost a lot. A complete, working item in good condition, with a buyer likely to want it and a manageable pickup, may justify a small listing trial. That is especially true when the owner wants to participate and someone has agreed to answer messages. The trial should have a stopping point already chosen with the owner. If the only evidence of value is the original receipt or a sibling’s memory of what it cost, don’t turn that into a family sales project.

If several attractive pieces need selling but the family doesn’t want to run listings, compare consignment with a company sale. A shop may suit selected items it already handles; an estate-sale company may suit a coherent collection it agrees to manage. Neither will necessarily accept everything. Get the selection, compensation, charges and unsold-item terms in writing. Count the heavy remainder in the decision, too.

Ask whether the family would still choose the route if the proceeds were lower than hoped. If not, pause for a better estimate or another destination. Don’t count the money toward the next home until the owner knows the expected amount, payment timing and charges.

For a category with several similar objects, make the first decision about the category, then the final decision item by item. The parent might approve trying one clean, working lamp for sale while choosing donation for the others. That small test gives the family evidence about messages, pickup effort and actual interest without committing the whole room. If there is no suitable response by the agreed review date, return to the parent with the original choices still visible. Don’t infer that silence means permission to lower the price or change the destination.

Keep the comparison on the amount and work the owner actually agreed to, not a hopeful gross figure. For a sale, note the expected proceeds, any agreed platform or service charges, who handles buyer contact and pickup, and the date the owner will decide whether to continue. For consignment or a sale company, use the written terms to identify when payment is expected and what costs may be deducted. For donation, record the confirmed recipient and the pickup or drop-off arrangement, not an assumed tax benefit. For removal, record the quoted charge and the exact items covered. These are different outcomes, so don’t make a donation appear cheaper by assigning it a guessed tax value or make a sale look better by ignoring the family’s time and the remaining items.

If a usable piece doesn’t justify a sale, donate only after a specific organization confirms it can take that item. Ask which recipient the parent prefers. If it declines, keep the item until another option is confirmed; a second call is easier than undoing a curbside pile.

If sale and donation fail, or an item is broken or difficult to move safely, compare removal options. Price the smallest scope that solves the problem: one item, several pieces or a room. Ask a municipal pickup, recycler, reuse service or paid crew what it handles. An itemized estimate should show included work, exclusions, and possible charges for stairs, distance, labor or disposal. Compare the written scope and its leftover plan, not just the total.

Before approval, review the removal list with the parent or authorized decision-maker. Name each item and mark what stays. “Everything in the basement” can include a tool the parent means to keep. Ask how the crew identifies approved items and handles a disagreement. If the family cannot resolve a question on arrival, that item stays.

Check timing and terms before booking: arrival window, payment trigger, cancellation or rescheduling, cleanup, and the plan for items refused. Get any change in writing before work begins. Don’t pay from the parent’s funds without approval and appropriate authority.

Sometimes the answer is a cost rather than proceeds. Record the scope and who will meet the crew. If the parent keeps an item, revise the list and price before loading; if the provider cannot revise its agreement, use another route or leave it in place.

The sequence fits in the margin of the room sheet: confirm ownership and approval; test a small sale only when buyer, labor and exit date make sense; compare written consignment or sale terms; donate to a confirmed recipient; price removal for the remainder. It isn’t a required ladder. Skip unlikely sales, don’t pay to remove an item accepted for donation, and use Chapter 12’s dated undecided box if the parent needs time.

The route belongs to the owner, not to the person with the truck. Treat each group as its own decision, and stop when the next step would require permission you do not have.

A computer needs a release check before it leaves

A laptop beside a donation carton may hold the only copy of your parent’s photographs. Its destination can be settled while its contents are not. Keep those as separate decisions. “Donate the computer” does not mean “erase everything today.”

Ask your parent what they still use it for and what they want to preserve. That might be photographs, correspondence, financial documents or a program they know how to use. Don’t let a replacement computer’s appearance convince you that the old one has become unnecessary. First ask your parent to show you how the important tasks will work on the replacement.

The Federal Trade Commission’s computer-disposal guidance, checked in 2026, puts backup before erasing the drive. It describes transferring files to another computer, using cloud storage, or saving to an external device. Let your parent choose a suitable method and who may help. Buying a storage device is not the same as putting the files on it.

Check the saved material before erasing anything. With permission, open a few important files from the backup location and confirm your parent can find them. A folder named “Dad’s photos” is not evidence that its contents copied successfully. If the family cannot tell whether the backup is usable, keep the old computer until a qualified technician can help.

This is not a reason for a sibling to gather every password. Ask your parent to enter private credentials themselves where possible. If someone must assist, agree on that specific task and keep access details out of the donation paperwork. A recipient needs to know the computer’s condition, not how to enter your parent’s email.

After the backup is confirmed, follow the device manufacturer’s current instructions for removing personal information. The FTC directs readers to the operating system’s drive-erasure and factory-reset tools. Use the directions for the actual computer; dragging visible documents into the trash is not the agency’s disposal procedure. Stop if an instruction is unclear rather than improvising because a pickup is coming.

An old computer that won’t start deserves the same pause. Don’t describe it as empty because the screen stays dark. Ask a qualified technician about preserving wanted files and removing personal information before release. If help is unavailable before the ordinary donation trip, leave that device behind for a separate, confirmed electronics route. Chapter 12’s special-handling boundary still applies.

Confirm whether the recipient accepts this model, in this condition, with its charger or other accessories. A useful description distinguishes working, untested and not working. Don’t advertise a reset machine as ready for every task your parent once performed on it, or promise that licensed software transfers with the hardware; check those terms with the provider.

For this item, the release note is simple: wanted files preserved and checked; personal-information removal completed using the applicable instructions; recipient and included accessories confirmed. It records what happened, not a promise that no data could ever be recovered.

Then the computer can join its approved load. Until then, an agreed destination is only half the answer.

A donation has to fit the recipient

Donation organizations set their own acceptance rules, which can change with space and need. One branch may accept furniture while another cannot; a group may take clean household goods and decline bulky or damaged items. Ask the specific site instead of testing with a loaded truck.

Call the actual location or pickup service. Describe the item’s condition, size and quantity, then ask whether it is accepted now, how to prepare it and whether pickup is available at your address. Confirm the date and limits before staging it.

Don’t leave goods outside a closed building or beside a donation bin. Ask where and when to bring them. If the organization says no, call another place; that’s not a judgment about your parent or the years they kept the object.

If your parent expects a tax benefit for donated property, don’t guess at a value or treat a donation receipt as a valuation. Ask a qualified tax professional what records and rules apply to your parent’s situation. This chapter is about finding an appropriate destination, not calculating a deduction.

When nobody wants the lot

Some houses contain more volume than resale value: boxes of books, dated linens, mismatched kitchenware, unsalable furniture and things nobody has identified. Don’t give away a whole truckload without first finding a willing recipient or service.

For usable books or household goods, try a library, school, community group, reuse center or charity shop. Ask about the exact material and quantity; none is obliged to take it. A place that accepts a few cartons may not have room for a vanload. A no rules out one route.

For a large collection, compare a sale company or auction service with other removal costs. Get a written estimate listing included work, possible added costs, leftover handling and the items the crew will remove. For junk removal, request an itemized price. A low quote isn’t comparable if it leaves heavy pieces or cleanup to your family.

Municipal bulk pickup, recycling and reuse programs vary by location. Contact the local public works or solid-waste office before setting anything at the curb; special items may need separate handling. Chapter 12 covers medicines, hazardous household products and important papers, which don’t belong in a general cleanout.

If the amount is too large to assess item by item, ask an estate-sale professional or cleanout service to explain its estimate. A community referral isn’t a collection promise. Don’t pay until your parent agrees to the scope and price and the person arranging it has authority.

Call before you haul

Keep this list beside the phone. Make a separate call for each destination; a yes from one branch doesn’t bind another.

  • What exactly is it? Give the item type, quantity, dimensions, condition and whether it works. Send a photo only if the organization offers a way to receive one.
  • Are you accepting it now? Ask about current limits rather than relying on the organization’s general mission.
  • What condition is acceptable? Ask about stains, wear, missing parts, repairs and whether the item needs to be clean or disassembled.
  • How much can you take? State the number of boxes or pieces and whether the load includes bulky furniture.
  • Is pickup available here? Confirm the address area, stairs or access issues, scheduling window, preparation and any pickup charge.
  • Where and when should a drop-off happen? Get the receiving entrance, days and hours, and ask whether an appointment is required.
  • What will you decline at the door? This gives you a chance to separate anything that cannot go on that trip.
  • Can you confirm the arrangement? Write down the contact, date and instructions; ask whether they can send the details in writing.
  • What is the backup for anything left behind? Decide on another confirmed destination or a quoted removal plan before loading.

For a company selling or removing property, add the business questions: what work is covered, what fees can change, who approves extra work, what happens to unsold items, how proceeds or charges are documented, and when the agreement ends. Take time to read the written terms. If they are unclear or the commitment is substantial, have an appropriate professional review them before your parent agrees.

Keep the destination with the load

Record the confirmed destination, approved items, pickup or removal date, and any unresolved question on the Chapter 10 work plan. The parent or authorized decision-maker approves written terms before an item leaves.

Don’t let the deadline choose for you

An approaching lease date or house closing can make every unsold item feel like an emergency. Divide the remaining work by destination and difficulty. Items already accepted for a confirmed pickup go in one group. Items with a likely buyer or a clear sale plan go in another. The unresolved pieces stay on a short list with one person assigned to get an answer. Keep the parent informed about the pace and ask what they are comfortable releasing.

Set a review date for items listed for sale. If there is no suitable response by then, ask the parent whether to change the price, try another route, or stop pursuing a sale. Don’t lower a price or give something away on their behalf simply because the family wants an empty room. Equally, don’t keep advertising an item indefinitely when the owner has chosen another destination and the family has a workable plan.

If a donation pickup is delayed, confirm the new date and what should happen in the meantime. If the organization cancels or changes its answer, the item stays put until a new destination is confirmed. That may mean calling another recipient, arranging a paid removal, or revisiting the schedule. It does not mean leaving the property at a curb or outside a closed building.

Sometimes the kindest answer is that the family will pay for removal rather than find a buyer or recipient for every last thing. Get a written, itemized quote, agree on precisely what the service may remove, and check that your parent approves the charge. A smaller pile of unresolved items is still a plan; it doesn’t have to be a heroic one.

The sleeper sofa did not become easier to donate because we had carried it to the truck. The useful part came later, when we started making calls before lifting anything. For the next load, write down one item, one destination to contact, and the person who will make that call. Leave the truck parked until you have an answer.

Chapter 14: Dividing Belongings Without a Family Fight

Curtis wanted the mantel clock. I wanted the mantel clock. Dad had already said we could work it out between us, so neither of us had said so out loud until we were both standing in front of it in his den. By then it had already stopped being about a clock.

We fixed it with stickers. Four colors, one roll of dot labels from the drugstore, and a round-robin where he picked, then I picked, then he picked again, until the family pile was gone. He got the clock on his third turn. Mom had agreed that her sewing table could go into the family pile; Dad offered the clock. I got the table on my second turn, which I’d actually wanted more and hadn’t said so either, because I was too busy wanting to win the clock.

That’s the whole lesson of this chapter, and I’ll say it early so you can stop reading if you’ve already got it: agree on a system before anyone starts picking. Not after somebody’s already carried something out to the car.

Why “whoever gets there first” causes trouble

Every family has a version of the story. A sibling arrives a day early and leaves with the good china. A sibling who lives closest quietly starts “holding onto” things weeks before anyone else gets a say. Nobody announced a rule, so everybody made one up, and the rules didn’t match.

First-come-first-served feels fair to the person who got there first. It feels like theft to everyone else. It rewards availability and proximity, not an agreed family process. None of that has anything to do with who should end up with Grandpa’s pocket watch.

The fix isn’t a complicated one. It’s deciding, as a family, on a method everybody agrees to use, before anyone touches the family pile. Once the method is set, the outcome belongs to the method, not to whoever grabbed fastest or complained loudest. Curtis didn’t get the clock because he wanted it more than I did. He got it because it was his turn.

This only works for the items in the family bucket from Chapter 12 — things somebody has actually asked for. Everything your parent is keeping, selling, or donating has already left the table. What’s left is the smaller, harder pile: the things more than one person in the family wants.

Three ways to divide, and how to pick one

There’s no single right system. There’s a right system for your family, your number of siblings, and how many items are actually in dispute. Here are three that work, in order of how much setup they take.

First ask your parent which items they want to offer and whether they want this division at all. If ownership or decision-making authority is unclear, stop and ask the appropriate attorney or authorized decision-maker. A sticker, a draft pick, or a tier assignment records a request, not permission to take an item.

Colored stickers and a round-robin

This is what Curtis and I used, and it’s the one I’d suggest if your family has three or more siblings and a modest number of contested items — a dozen or two, not a houseful.
