Give each person a different color of dot sticker. Everybody walks the house separately, before any picking starts, and puts their color on anything they’d like to have, with no limit and no discussion yet. An item might end up with one sticker, three stickers, or none.

Anything with exactly one sticker is an uncontested request; confirm the parent’s approval before recording who takes it. That’s usually most of the pile. It’s the overlapping stickers, two colors on the same item, that need the round-robin.

Put the contested items in one list. Draw an order (oldest to youngest, a coin flip, whatever your family won’t argue about later), and go around in turns. First person picks one item from the contested list. Second person picks one. Keep going, looping back to the start, until the contested list is empty. Write down who picked what and in which round as you go — you’ll want that record later, and nobody remembers accurately a year from now.

The stickers make the preferences visible before the draft, so the family can see which items actually need a turn. Seeing that an item has only your sticker on it settles most of the house without a single turn being taken.

A straight draft

If your family is smaller, two or three people, or the contested pile is long, skip the stickers and draft directly. Put every item that more than one person wants on a single numbered list. Decide the order the same way (oldest first is the old standby, and it has the advantage of nobody arguing about it). Then go around picking one item per turn, looping until the list is empty, same as above.

A draft is faster to set up than stickers because you skip the walk-through. It front-loads more decision-making: everybody has to agree on the full contested list before anyone picks. That means somebody has to ask, out loud, “does anyone else want this?” for every borderline item. That conversation is useful, even when it’s a little awkward. It’s much better to have it standing in the den than over a group text three weeks later.

A simple rotation by value tier

For a larger estate with real differences in value among the contested items, not just the clock but also a car, some jewelry, and a set of tools, a flat round-robin can hand one person three small things while someone else gets the one expensive item, and call it even when it wasn’t.

If that’s your situation, sort the contested items into rough tiers first, high, medium, low, by family agreement, not appraisal. Then draft within each tier, rotating the pick order between tiers so the same person isn’t always choosing first. Someone who picks first in the high tier picks last in the medium tier. The point is to set a process the family can explain and follow before the first pick.

Whichever method you choose, put it in writing before the first pick, and get everyone’s agreement on it — including anyone who isn’t in the room for the actual dividing. A method agreed to after the fact, by the person who lost a pick, isn’t really agreed to.

The one item two people both want

Even with a method running smoothly, a single item sometimes won’t let go. Two people both want the same ring, the same tools, the same photograph of a parent as a young person. A round-robin resolves most things by handing them to whoever’s turn it is. It doesn’t make anyone stop wanting what they didn’t get.

A few ways through it, roughly in order of how much they ask of everyone:

Ask what it’s for. The same question from Chapter 12’s load-bearing items works here too. Sometimes two people want the same ring for different reasons — one wants to wear it, one wants it because their mother wore it in a photograph they love. Once you know why, there’s often a second item that answers the same need: a different piece of jewelry, a copy of the photograph, a story written down. Not every want needs the exact object to be satisfied.

Split the physical thing if it can be split without ruining it. A large photograph can be copied. A set of flatware can be divided into two smaller sets. A collection of tools can be split by type. This doesn’t work for a clock or a wedding ring, but it solves more disputes than people expect, because families often fight over “the set” when what they actually want is “some of it.”

Let it rotate on a schedule. For something nobody’s willing to give up and that can’t be split, a few families agree to share it: a holiday centerpiece that travels house to house each year, a quilt that moves between two homes on alternating years. This takes an ongoing level of goodwill that not every family has, and it needs a clear plan for who holds it and for how long, written down the same way everything else in this chapter gets written down. If that plan isn’t realistic for your family, don’t adopt it to avoid a harder conversation. An unrealistic shared-custody arrangement for a mantel clock usually just moves the argument five years down the road.

Ask your parent to decide, while they’re able to and willing to. This is worth trying earlier than families usually try it. A parent who has strong feelings about where a specific item should go, and is willing to say so, settles the question in a way no sticker or draft can touch. The parent decides while able and willing. The authority here still belongs to your parent, same as every other decision in this book — their preference for an item isn’t a tiebreaker the siblings get to overrule once they hear it.

If none of that resolves it and the item may have real financial value, pause the informal process. Confirm who owns it and who has authority to act; then ask the attorney or fiduciary already handling the parent’s estate or trust whether an appraisal, a parent-approved sale, or another documented resolution is appropriate under your state’s law.

What doesn’t help: the person who wants it most “needing” it more because of a harder year, a rockier marriage, or more kids who’ll “appreciate it.” Weighing who deserves an object based on whose life looks harder from the outside is a scale with no bottom, and somebody always loses on it twice — once on the item, and again on being told their life wasn’t hard enough to earn it.

Write down who got what

Curtis and I wrote nothing down. We remembered the clock and the sewing table because those were the items with feelings attached. We did not remember, a year later, who ended up with Mom’s good scissors or the box of canning jars, and it didn’t matter, because nobody was keeping score on scissors.

Somebody will keep score eventually, though, usually on something that mattered more than scissors. Write down, as you go, a short list: item, who got it, and the date. It doesn’t need to be formal. A page in a notebook or a shared document works. What matters is that it exists, so that six months from now, if someone asks “didn’t I pick the desk lamp?”, there’s an answer that isn’t four people’s competing memories.

Use Chapter 10’s existing sheet for the family-pile division; keep the approved picks beside that entry.

An able parent makes or approves the disposition; their preferences get written down too, in the same list, same as a sibling’s pick. This isn’t a legal document and it doesn’t need a lawyer’s involvement for ordinary household items. If anything in the contested pile is genuinely valuable, real jewelry, art, a collection with real market worth, that’s a different conversation. It belongs with whoever is already handling your parent’s estate planning, not worked out informally over a weekend with stickers.

Pick a system before anyone picks an item

Here’s the short version, the one-page guide to tape to the fridge before the first sticker goes on anything:

First confirm which items your parent has offered and who may authorize their disposition; a draft records requests until the owner or authorized decision-maker approves them.

  • Colored stickers plus round-robin. Best for three or more people and a modest contested pile. Walk the house separately first, mark anything you’d want, then draft the overlaps in turns.
  • Straight draft. Best for two or three people, or a long contested list. Agree the full list out loud first, then draft in turns.
  • Tiered rotation. Best when contested items vary a lot in value. Sort into rough tiers by agreement, then draft within each tier with the pick order flipped between tiers.

Agree on the method before anyone starts. Set the pick order before anyone knows who benefits. Record each result as you go. For one item that remains contested, use the earlier list. Ask what it is for. See whether it can be split. Consider rotation only if it is realistic. Ask the parent while they can answer. Consult the estate attorney if a buyout is necessary.

Before the first sticker goes on an item, name the method, the pick order, and the person recording the result. That is enough to turn a tense pile into a process.

Chapter 15: Hiring Movers Without Getting Scammed

A phone-only quote, a large cash deposit, an incomplete bill of lading, or no physical address is a reason to pause. Ask for a written estimate after an in-person or live-video survey, verify the interstate carrier or broker through FMCSA — or the state regulator for a wholly in-state move — and compare complete terms before booking.

The company with the truck, and the company arranging it

An estimate may come from a moving company or a broker. A mover has trucks and moving staff and takes responsibility for transport. A broker arranges transportation; it does not own the truck or employ the crew carrying the furniture. It is not the company loading the china cabinet.

That difference changes the questions to ask. According to the FMCSA’s Movers vs. Brokers guidance, both interstate movers and brokers must be registered. A broker must identify itself as an arranger, provide the movers it uses, and have a written agreement with the carrier. Its estimate must be based on that mover’s tariff. The mover performs a physical survey unless you choose to waive it. These are interstate requirements; for an in-state move, check the relevant state regulator’s rules.

Before comparing prices, ask for the carrier’s name and USDOT number, whether it is selected, and how the broker will report a change. Check both businesses through FMCSA’s Protect Your Move search. A broker’s registration doesn’t establish the carrier’s suitability or make its estimate a full service description.

Ask who conducts the survey and when the carrier sees the home and inventory. If asked to waive it, understand what you give up and how the estimate was prepared. Don’t leave missing details for the crew to resolve at the curb, when you may discover the carrier priced a different shipment.

Before signing, read the broker’s agreement and the estimate. Confirm that the broker arranges rather than transports, identify the expected carrier, and check what each company agreed to do if the assignment changes. Keep contact details for both. The broker’s agreement and carrier’s estimate are separate records.

Some families prefer the carrier directly; others value help finding one. Compare written responsibilities, identified carrier, survey, charges and contact path. Get missing or changed terms in writing before paying or signing.

Put the estimates on the same page

Each estimate should price substantially the same move. One company may count the garage and patio furniture; another may price only the rooms named on a phone call. Its lower total then answers a different question.

Start with each survey inventory. Check rooms and note essential or bulky pieces, packed boxes, fragile property and items staying behind. The list needn’t name every spoon, but it should capture goods that affect truck size, labor, packing, handling or storage. Get omissions corrected in writing before comparing totals.

Line up services: loading only, or packing and materials too? Are disassembly, stairs, long carries, shuttle equipment or difficult access priced separately? Who packs fragile pieces? If the parent cannot take delivery on arrival, is storage included, for how long, and who handles delivery later? Mark each item included, separately priced, excluded or unanswered. An unanswered service isn’t free.

For each offer, mark binding or non-binding and copy the quantities and services that define its price. According to FMCSA’s glossary, a binding estimate fixes the cost for the described quantities and services. Added goods or services can require another agreement. A non-binding interstate estimate is the mover’s prediction; final charges depend on actual shipment weight, services and tariff terms. Ask the company to explain which basis it used. For an in-state move, check your state’s estimate rules instead.

FMCSA’s guidance, checked in 2026, describes the 110 percent rule for collection at delivery on a non-binding interstate estimate. Do not treat it as a ceiling on every possible final charge. Ask the carrier how the rule applies to the proposed shipment, including requested additions and later billing, before counting on a particular balance.

That distinction matters in a comparison without making one estimate type automatically better. A binding offer for loading only is not equivalent to a non-binding offer that includes packing. First match the work. Then ask what cost uncertainty remains under each complete offer and whether your parent is comfortable with it. If the company cannot explain the price basis in terms your parent understands, keep that offer undecided.

Record pickup and delivery windows, how the company characterizes delivery, and its response if dates shift. Note who arranges storage if the parent cannot receive the shipment, and each contact’s name, role and number. List a broker and carrier separately. If responsibility or governing documents are unclear, ask before the deposit.

Compare protection as well as premium. For interstate moves, ask for the default valuation, alternatives, limits, cost and any required election. State rules vary for in-state moves; ask the regulator. Compare offers only after you understand what the selected protection means for valued belongings.

The simplest working sheet has one column per company and rows for carrier or broker, survey, inventory gaps, estimate type, included services, separate charges, dates, storage, protection, unanswered questions and total. Give each business the same questions and ask for written corrections. Hold incomplete offers aside until terms arrive. A lower number can be reasonable when scope and written answers match; otherwise it is not a meaningful comparison.

Buy a finished service, not an unexplained verb

“Move the bedroom” can mean carrying furniture or leaving a usable bed assembled in the new room. Those aren’t the same purchase. Ask where the crew’s job ends. If the quoted work includes disassembly but not reassembly, decide whether that offer actually suits your parent before comparing it with a company that does both.

Take one awkward piece through the proposed service from beginning to end. Suppose a glass-front cabinet has removable shelves and a narrow stair landing at the old address. Ask who removes and packs the shelves, how the cabinet travels, and who puts it back together. Ask whether crating or a separate specialist is proposed. You are buying an explanation, not prescribing a lifting technique to the crew.

At the other end, describe the actual entrance. A model apartment tour doesn’t tell a mover about a delivery door, elevator reservation or restricted truck access. Obtain the building’s delivery instructions and pass them to the company before deciding on the service. The FMCSA’s moving glossary identifies additional services such as stair carries and shuttle transport; those words describe work that can carry separate charges.

A practical question is: “With these entrance instructions and this cabinet, what will your crew do, and what would require another provider?” If the answer involves a third party, ask who hires that provider and whether its charge appears in the mover’s total. Don’t accept two offers as equivalent when one assumes the family supplies a missing service.

Appliances need their own answer. Ask which preparation or reconnection tasks the mover performs, and which need a qualified service technician. Don’t assume someone carrying a washer will disconnect plumbing or reconnect it. This is a scope question, not an invitation for your family to learn electrical work during a move.

Unpacking can also stop sooner than you imagine. Does the service remove things from cartons, place them where instructed, or take away empty packaging? Ask about each part you want. A parent who cannot handle cartons after delivery needs an actual arrangement, not the word “unpacking” in a sales conversation.

You can decline extras. You cannot compare a finished room with a stack of boxes as if they were the same job.

Storage has an exit as well as an entrance

If storage is needed, ask whether the proposal is temporary storage during transport or a separate storage contract. The FMCSA glossary calls temporary warehouse holding before further delivery “storage-in-transit.” Find out what arrangement the company is offering rather than using that label for every warehouse stay.

Ask what causes the arrangement to change: the period ending, a missed delivery appointment, or a request for longer storage. Request the applicable charges and protection terms for each stage. Don’t assume the transport terms continue unchanged under a new agreement.

The useful question isn’t only “Where is the warehouse?” It is “Can my parent retrieve a particular carton, and what does that involve?” A stored shipment may not be arranged like a family-accessible storage locker. Confirm whether access is offered, how it is requested, what it costs, and whether someone must locate and bring out the goods. An address does not promise access.

Ask about redelivery separately from storage rent. What notice does the company need when the new room becomes available? Is a second delivery charge included? Would a different crew or carrier handle it? Have the company identify the document governing that leg and the contact who schedules it.

For a hypothetical apartment awaiting a repair, the family might know the earliest possible occupancy date but not the actual date. Tell the mover that distinction. Ask for storage and redelivery terms suitable for an unconfirmed release date instead of booking a delivery nobody can yet receive. Chapter 17 handles the parent’s arrival; this decision is about custody of the goods.

Know what each paper records

An estimate describes proposed charges. An inventory identifies the goods and can record their condition. The bill of lading is the transport contract and receipt for the shipment, according to the FMCSA’s moving glossary. One document cannot stand in for the other two.

When papers use different descriptions, have the company explain the difference. A bedroom dresser on the inventory should be recognizable as the piece included in the accepted service. An unexplained switch from the company you selected to another carrier needs attention, not an assumption that the logo on the folder covers everyone involved.

Ask for the abbreviations used on the inventory before there is a crowded loading doorway. Condition codes should mean something to the parent reading them. If a notation says a table was scratched before loading and you disagree, ask to have the specific disagreement recorded. “Furniture looks fine” is less useful than identifying the piece and the disputed mark.

The FMCSA’s consumer-rights page says interstate movers and brokers must provide Your Rights and Responsibilities When You Move and the Ready to Move brochure. It also describes written complaint procedures and a contact number. Read those materials before accepting the company’s agreement; they explain more than a salesperson’s reassurance can.

Use Chapter 10’s booking entry for the accepted offer. Keep an accessible copy of the transport papers outside the shipment, with your parent’s private information protected. A folder locked inside the furniture truck cannot answer a question about that truck.

Payment questions that belong before the move

Ask who receives each payment. A broker fee, a carrier deposit and a delivery balance may be separate amounts under separate agreements. Request an explanation showing which amount, if any, is credited against another. Don’t subtract a broker payment from the carrier’s balance just because it feels like part of one bill.

Then ask what event makes each payment due and what happens if the customer cancels. Read the actual refund and cancellation language. A change in the parent’s housing date is a reason to understand those terms, not proof of a refund right. State rules and the type of shipment matter; ask the relevant regulator about requirements you cannot interpret.

Confirm the accepted payment method and any preparation needed for delivery. Don’t assume the card used for a deposit can automatically pay the balance, or that a personal check will be accepted. The answer should come from the company handling the charge. Keep account information off a general sibling thread.

If a document creates an unclear personal payment obligation for you, ask an appropriate attorney before signing. Taking the parent’s phone calls isn’t the same as agreeing to pay their bill. The family authority boundary remains the one in Chapter 10.

Basic coverage isn’t the same as full value

For an interstate move, Full Value Protection applies unless the customer signs for Released Value, the free but minimal per-pound option. Ask for both written descriptions and costs. In-state rules vary, so verify them with the state regulator. A lamp and a clock of the same weight receive the same weight-based limit under Released Value, even if their market values differ. Your parent should understand that trade-off before making the election.

The FMCSA’s Liability & Protection page, checked in 2026, explains that Full Value Protection can involve repair, replacement with a similar item, or a cash settlement. It doesn’t promise recovery of sentimental value. Ask about deductibles and the written method for resolving damage; “full” doesn’t mean every loss is settled on your preferred terms.

The same page warns about failing to identify articles of extraordinary value in writing. Ask the mover to explain its declaration form and the applicable limitation, then help your parent identify any pieces requiring that disclosure. A photo attached to a family message isn’t the same as a declaration on the shipping documents. Have the company show where the accepted declaration appears.

Photographs help describe condition. With your parent’s permission, take views that identify the whole piece and any existing damage, rather than only the attractive side. For an electronic item, note the identifying model or serial number privately if available. Don’t put photographs of jewelry or account records in the album everybody uses for moving progress.

For fragile owner-packed cartons, ask what evidence would be useful if damage is discovered. FMCSA warns that packing your own goods can make a claim harder to establish. That is not a statement that every owner-packed item is excluded. Read the actual terms and don’t infer either automatic payment or automatic rejection.

Prepare for a damaged or missing item without assuming one

Ask for the claim form and submission instructions while arranging the service. That request isn’t an accusation. It is finding the process before the parent needs it. Save the carrier’s claim contact separately from a broker’s booking contact; the person who arranged the shipment may not decide a damage claim.

If a problem occurs, describe the item and what happened, keeping copies of the inventory, transport contract, photographs and relevant messages. Ask the carrier what supporting documents it needs and how it confirms receipt. An initial phone conversation can start the inquiry, but it doesn’t replace following the written claim procedure.

FMCSA’s liability page states, as checked in 2026, that a written loss-or-damage claim must be filed with the mover within nine months after delivery. Report a problem promptly rather than treating that outside limit as a reason to wait. For an in-state shipment, ask the state regulator about the applicable process and deadline; do not carry the federal period over by assumption.

The agency’s dispute guidance describes arbitration and legal action for unresolved interstate disputes. It also says FMCSA cannot act as your advocate against the mover or enforce a court judgment. A regulatory complaint and recovery of your parent’s loss are separate matters. Ask the regulator and, for a contested substantial loss, an appropriate attorney which steps apply. This book doesn’t decide liability or tell you to accept a settlement.

A short verification checklist

Before you book anyone, moving a single state or several:

FMCSA’s glossary includes a shipment between points in one state that travels through another state in its interstate definition. Ask about the route, not just the two addresses, before choosing the branch below.

If the move crosses a state line:

  • Get the company’s USDOT number
  • Look it up at fmcsa.dot.gov/protect-your-move
  • Confirm active registration and check the complaint history
  • Don’t book if the number doesn’t check out or the company won’t provide one

If the move stays within one state:

  • Identify your state’s moving or household-goods regulator (your state consumer protection office can point you there if you’re not sure)
  • Confirm the company’s standing with that state agency
  • Don’t skip this step just because there’s no federal registration to check

Either way, in writing:

  • A binding or non-binding estimate, itemized
  • Pickup and delivery dates, with a stated consequence for delays
  • Payment schedule and method, with real caution toward a large cash deposit
  • A complete bill of lading before the truck is loaded, not after
  • A confirmed physical address and phone number for the company

Open the accepted service description with your parent. Point to where the crew’s work ends. If a usable bed or a stored carton falls outside it, resolve that missing service before the booking.

Chapter 16: The House Sale

In an illustrative comparison, a contractor’s written roof quote and an agent’s written as-is estimate pointed in different directions. The owner chose the option that fit the move’s timing after reviewing both documents.

That’s most of what this chapter is: getting the numbers and the paperwork in front of you before the family argues about what to do with the house. It’s usually the biggest asset in the move, and the one everyone has an opinion about without having the facts.

As-is or fixed up first

Every house has a list. Dad’s had a roof, a water heater nobody trusted, and a den carpet that still smelled like the dog who’d been gone eleven years. The question isn’t whether the list is real. It’s whether fixing it before you sell actually makes the family more money, or just makes the family feel better about selling a house with problems.

That’s a real estate agent’s question to answer with a number, not a family’s question to answer with a feeling. Ask directly whether a candidate agent has handled moves like this one, because plenty haven’t. A good agent who has will walk the house with you and point out, item by item, which repairs a buyer or lender is likely to care about. Do not assume a roof, driveway, or other repair pays for itself. Compare a qualified contractor’s written scope and quote with the agent’s written as-is and repaired market estimates, then let the owner decide after seeing expected net proceeds and timing.

Ask a qualified inspector or contractor for that repair list in writing, item by item, with their estimate of what each repair costs. Then ask the agent for a separate written estimate of what each repair is likely to add to the sale price. A buyer’s taste-based objection and a condition issue can call for different written questions. Ask the agent what the inspection response, offer terms, and any lender-related conditions require for this sale. There’s a second, quieter question underneath the first: how much is the family’s time and the parent’s patience worth, measured against a few thousand dollars either way? Ask for the proposed repair schedule before deciding whether it fits the move.

Selling as-is isn’t a lesser option. It’s a legitimate choice when the family doesn’t have the time, the cash, or the stomach to manage a renovation during an already hard season. A good agent will say so plainly. Ask the agent to disclose compensation and explain each repair recommendation in writing; compare that recommendation with the independent contractor quotes. Then put the as-is numbers and the fixed-up numbers side by side and let the actual numbers settle the argument that would otherwise happen in the driveway.

Finding an agent who’s done this before

Not every real estate agent has sold a house out from under a parent moving to assisted living, and the ones who haven’t will sometimes treat it like any other listing: stage it, list it, sell it, done. That’s fine if your family’s timeline is ordinary. It often isn’t.

Ask a candidate agent directly: have you sold a house for a family in the middle of a parent’s move before? How do you coordinate a closing date with a move-in date that isn’t fully in your control? What do you do if the facility has a waiting list and the house sale needs to happen faster than the market wants to move? Ask each candidate to explain a prior coordination problem, the proposed timeline for this sale, and the backup plan if dates separate. Check references and judge the specificity of the answer rather than experience language alone — a vague answer here is how families end up paying for a month of overlapping rent and mortgage, or rushing a sale for less than it was worth.

Get the agent’s commission structure and the listing agreement in writing before signing anything, and ask who signs it — this matters more here than in an ordinary sale, because of the authority question that opened Chapter 10. The person who signs a listing agreement, and later a closing document, has to actually hold the legal authority to do it. If your parent is selling their own house and is able to sign for themselves, that’s the straightforward answer. If someone else holds signing authority for the parent, confirm with an elder law attorney, before the listing goes live, that the specific document authorizes a real estate sale and that it’s current and properly executed. This isn’t a job for a family’s best guess, and it isn’t a job for the real estate agent either — an agent sells houses; a lawyer confirms who’s allowed to sign for one.

What the IRS actually says about the tax

Most families have heard something about not paying tax on a home sale. Fewer have heard the actual rule, and fewer still have checked whether a parent’s specific situation meets it, which is the part that gets missed when the broad version gets passed around a family group text as settled fact.

The 2025 Publication 523 says the maximum exclusion can be up to $250,000, or up to $500,000 on a qualifying joint return. Generally, the taxpayer must have owned the home for at least 24 months in the five years before sale and used it as a main home for at least 24 months in that period. The periods need not coincide. The look-back, disqualifications, joint-return rules and possible exceptions still require review under the current Publication 523. Ownership and residence are only part of the Eligibility Test. Confirm the automatic disqualifications and the two-year look-back too. For the $500,000 joint-return maximum, both spouses generally must meet the residence and look-back requirements. At least one spouse must also meet ownership. Have the tax professional apply the current publication’s complete test to the actual sale, not a family’s shorthand version of it.

Publication 523 also states a narrower rule for a family in this exact situation. If the taxpayer became unable to care for themself, time in a care facility can sometimes count toward the home-use side of the Eligibility Test. Three conditions have to be true for that to apply. The parent must have been physically or mentally unable to care for themself. The home must have been used as a main home for at least twelve months within the five years before the sale. The facility must be licensed by a state or other political entity to care for people with that specific condition. Miss any one of those conditions and this narrower rule doesn’t apply.

Whether a particular parent’s situation satisfies all three isn’t something to settle around the kitchen table from memory of what a cousin’s accountant once said. The dollar amounts, the five-year window, and the facility-licensing question depend on facts specific to your parent’s history and your state’s facility-licensing categories. Name the rule to your tax professional and let them confirm whether your parent’s house sale actually qualifies, and for how much. A CPA or tax professional who prepares the actual return answers this, not a real estate agent, and not this book.

What a tax professional and a real estate agent each actually handle

It helps to know, before either phone call, which question belongs to which person. Families sometimes ask the real estate agent a tax question and the tax question goes unanswered. Or they ask the CPA a repair-pricing question and get a shrug.

A qualified inspector or contractor handles: assessing the condition of each repair item and providing a written cost estimate. That cost estimate is theirs to give, not the agent’s and not the family’s.

The real estate agent handles: pricing the house as-is and with repairs completed (market-value scenarios, not repair cost estimates), finding and vetting buyers, negotiating the sale price and terms, coordinating the closing date against the move-in date, and the listing agreement itself.

The tax professional handles: whether the home-sale exclusion applies to this specific sale, and whether the Eligibility Test is met in full. They also confirm whether the care-facility exception applies and whether its three conditions are satisfied. And they determine the adjusted basis, any effect of repairs or improvements on it, and what (if anything) is owed and reported on the parent’s tax return for that year.

A real estate attorney, separate from both, handles reviewing the purchase contract and closing documents, confirming who actually holds signing authority for the parent, and any title or deed question the closing turns up. Which professional handles this depends on state practice — some states route it through a title company instead of an attorney. If the signing-authority question from Chapter 10 is anything less than fully settled, escalate to that attorney or title professional. The same goes for a title wrinkle — an old lien, a name that doesn’t match current records, a deed held jointly with someone who’s since died. That’s not the agent’s question to answer, and it isn’t the CPA’s either.

Ask each professional the question that belongs to their role, and don’t let any one of them answer for the others, even if they’re confident. An agent who tells you the tax exclusion “definitely applies” is being generous with an opinion that isn’t theirs to give.

A worksheet for both calls

Before you call the tax professional and the real estate agent, write down what you actually need from each one. It keeps the calls short and keeps you from hanging up having talked for twenty minutes about something neither of you needed answered today.

For the real estate agent:

  • What would this house sell for as-is, today, in writing?
  • What would it sell for with the repair list completed? (Get repair costs separately from a qualified contractor, not from the agent.)
  • Which repairs affect financing, not just a buyer’s taste?
  • What’s a realistic timeline from listing to closing, given the current market?
  • Can the closing date be coordinated against a move-in date, and how much flexibility is there on either end?
  • Have you managed this kind of move-timed sale before, and what went wrong the last time?
  • Who signs the listing agreement, and has that person’s authority to sign been confirmed?

For the tax professional:

  • What edition of Publication 523 are you using? Does this sale meet the complete Eligibility Test — ownership, residence, the two-year look-back, and the automatic disqualifications — not just the two-of-five-year ownership and use test?
  • Has either spouse excluded gain on another home sale within the two years before this closing, and does that affect the look-back?
  • For a joint return, do both spouses meet the residence and look-back requirements, and does at least one meet ownership?
  • If my parent has spent time in a care facility, does the twelve-month prior main-home use condition hold, and is the facility licensed in the way the care-facility exception requires?
  • What is the adjusted basis, and what records of the purchase price, capital improvements, and selling expenses do you need to calculate it?
  • Does the new roof, or any other repair made before the sale, count as a capital improvement that changes adjusted basis? (Confirm the answer with the tax professional; don’t calculate this yourselves.)
  • Was the home ever used for business or rental purposes, and does depreciation taken reduce the excludable gain?
  • Given all of that, how much of the gain, if any, is excludable, and how much (if any) is taxable?
  • Will we receive Form 1099-S, and does the sale need to be reported on the return even if the gain is fully excludable?
  • What records do you need from us before the sale closes, and what records do you need afterward for the return?
  • Does the timing of the sale within this calendar year matter for anything else in my parent’s tax situation?

Write down who’s calling each professional and by what date, using the owner-and-due-date habit Chapter 10 already set up for every other task. Keep both professionals’ written answers in the same place the family already keeps receipts and quotes. A tax answer given over the phone and never written down has a way of getting half-remembered by the time the return is actually filed.

The records folder before you list

Before the sign goes in the yard, the agent and the tax professional will both ask for paper you may not have gathered yet. Keep it in the same folder Chapter 10 already set up for receipts and quotes, with its own labeled section, rather than digging for it the week of closing.

For the agent and any buyer’s inspector, collect the deed, the most recent property tax bill, the most recent mortgage statement if one exists, and any survey or lot map already on file. Add warranty information for a furnace, water heater or roof replaced within the last several years, along with the contractor’s name and the date the work was done. A documented recent replacement is often worth more to an agent building a case for the asking price than a parent would expect, especially once a buyer’s inspector flags the same system as original. If the house has had a well, septic system, or any structural repair, gather those records specifically; they come up in inspections more often than families expect and are harder to produce after the fact than before.

For the tax professional, collect the original purchase settlement statement or closing disclosure, with the purchase price. Add receipts or invoices for capital improvements going back as far as records exist: a new roof, an addition, a kitchen remodel, replacement windows. These can change the adjusted basis the tax professional calculates. Routine repairs and maintenance, as the tax professional will confirm, are a different category from capital improvements and are tracked separately; don’t guess which pile a given receipt belongs in. If the house was ever rented out or used for any business purpose, gather whatever depreciation records exist from those years; the tax professional needs them even if the rental period ended long ago.

If a parent no longer has some of these records, that’s common, not disqualifying. A title company or the county recorder’s office can often supply a copy of the deed and past tax records. A mortgage lender, if the loan is still active, can supply a current statement. None of this has to be perfect before the first call to the agent or the tax professional — it has to exist before the closing, and starting the search now beats searching for it under deadline pressure in the final week.

Questions for the week of closing

The numbers worksheet earlier in this chapter covers what to ask before you sign anything. A second, shorter set of questions matters once a buyer is under contract and a closing date is on the calendar, because this is where a parent’s move-in date and the house sale’s timeline either line up or collide.

Ask the agent or the closing company handling the transaction:

  • What is the exact closing date, and how much can it move if the parent’s new living arrangement isn’t ready on that day?
  • What repairs, if any, came out of the buyer’s inspection, and who is paying for them? Get this in writing before assuming the sale price is final.
  • Is the closing in person or remote, and does the parent need to be physically present, or can a power of attorney or other authorized signer handle it if the parent’s travel is limited? Confirm this with the real estate attorney or title company handling the closing, not with the agent.
  • When do sale proceeds actually arrive, and in whose name or account? If proceeds are needed to cover a deposit or first month at the next home, confirm the timing lines up before counting on same-day funds.
  • What final utility, HOA, or property-tax prorations happen at closing, and is there anything the family needs to cancel or transfer afterward, such as mail forwarding, homeowner’s insurance, or utility accounts, that doesn’t happen automatically?

Ask the title company or real estate attorney whether title, signing arrangements, occupancy, insurance, or proceeds timing creates a risk for this closing. Get the answer and relevant deadlines in writing.

Write the answers down, with the name of whoever gave them, in the same place the family is tracking everything else from Chapter 10’s work plan. A closing date that slips by two weeks is a scheduling problem if the family knows about it early. It’s a crisis if it surfaces the day before a moving truck is already booked.

Read the seller’s money sheet, not just the price

A buyer’s offer and the amount your parent can use after closing are different questions. Ask the agent or settlement professional for a seller’s estimated net-proceeds statement appropriate to this transaction. Treat it as an estimate, with its assumptions visible, rather than money already in the bank.

Have the professional walk through the deductions shown: agreed selling charges, any loan payoff, credits negotiated with the buyer, and other transaction adjustments. Ask which figures are confirmed and which are provisional. Don’t replace a missing payoff figure with the balance from an old statement or assume a buyer credit is already included because everyone discussed it.

If the repair choice changes, ask for the revised seller estimate. A higher sale price does not answer the comparison if preparing that version requires additional spending. Keep pre-sale expenses visible beside the seller statement and ask which are already reflected in it. This is how you avoid counting a contractor’s invoice twice, or forgetting it entirely.

The tax calculation is separate. The IRS’s 2025 Publication 523, rechecked in 2026, figures gain from the amount realized after selling expenses, less adjusted basis. The deposit arriving after closing is not a substitute for that calculation. Give the tax professional the completed transaction papers and let them distinguish sale cash from gain; don’t apply the exclusion to a bank deposit yourselves.

Before funds are committed to the next home, ask the tax professional whether any amount should remain available for obligations arising from this sale. Ask the settlement professional when the seller’s funds will be released and the receiving bank when they can be used. Neither an offer acceptance nor a signing appointment answers all three questions.

Confirm the path for closing funds

Ask the settlement professional how payment instructions are exchanged and verified for this sale. Keep the verified contact information separately from incoming messages. Your parent’s account details belong in the agreed secure process, not copied to everybody who has helped clear the house.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s archived mortgage-closing scam guidance describes false wiring instructions in messages impersonating trusted closing professionals. Its advice is to confirm instructions in person or through a previously agreed phone number, not a number or link supplied by the message. That page addresses buyers; for this seller’s transaction, ask the settlement professional how to authenticate any payment request or change to proceeds instructions.

If a message proposes a new account or a last-minute transfer, stop the transaction instruction long enough to verify it independently. Call the known settlement contact. Don’t reply to the suspicious message asking whether it is real; that leaves the same sender answering the question. An urgent tone is not confirmation.

If money has already been sent under suspected false instructions, contact the bank or wire-transfer provider immediately and ask about a recall. CFPB’s guidance also directs victims to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center. Tell the real settlement professional what happened. Do not assume reporting recovers the funds, or delay the bank call while the family investigates by text.

What this chapter isn’t

This chapter is not a Medicaid or estate-planning guide. The house sale question sits right next to both of those without actually being either one. Selling a parent’s house can affect eligibility for programs with their own financial rules. A house held in certain kinds of estate planning may carry its own sale restrictions, entirely separate from the IRS exclusion discussed here. Both of those are real questions for some families. Neither is answered in this book. If either one applies to your parent, an elder law attorney is who untangles it. The sooner that conversation happens relative to the sale, the more options usually stay open.

This chapter also isn’t where you compare the cost of the next home against the cost of staying — that math belongs to Chapter 11’s worksheet, built on written local quotes, not a house-sale number. What this chapter hands you is the other half: a clear, sourced answer about the tax exclusion, a way to choose between as-is and fixed-up, and a short list of who to call and what to ask them. Because the house may be one of the parent’s largest assets, use documented figures and professional answers rather than family guesses.

Put the contractor’s scope beside the agent’s market estimate. Ask your parent which missing answer they need before choosing.

Chapter 17: Moving Day

In one composite move, a daughter ran her father’s move like a wedding she’d spent a year planning, right down to a laminated schedule taped to the refrigerator. Eight-thirty, movers arrive. Nine, bedroom loaded. Eleven, kitchen loaded. The truck pulled out at one o’clock, on time, exactly as written. Her father sat in a folding chair in the empty living room the whole morning, watching his furniture leave through the front door, and by noon he wasn’t speaking to anyone. The schedule had worked perfectly. It just hadn’t accounted for the fact that he was watching his house disappear in real time while everyone around him moved briskly from room to room like it was any other Tuesday.

Put one person beside your parent from eight to noon. Their only job is to notice when the day has become too much.

What the day is actually for

By the time moving day arrives, the hard decisions are behind you. The sorting is done, the dividing is settled, the movers are vetted and booked, the house sale paperwork is in motion or already signed. Moving day itself isn’t a decision day. It’s an execution day, and the best moving days are the boring ones, where nothing has to be decided on the spot because it was already decided weeks earlier.

That’s worth saying plainly because families sometimes save decisions for moving day without meaning to — “we’ll figure out which boxes go where once we’re there,” or “Dad can decide what stays out when he sees the new place.” Don’t do that to moving day. It has enough to carry already. Anything that can be decided before the truck shows up should be decided before the truck shows up.

Reducing a parent’s anxiety on the day itself

A parent’s anxiety on moving day rarely looks like anxiety from the outside. It looks like irritability over a small thing — a box packed the wrong way, a chair moved before they were ready to say goodbye to where it had always sat. It looks like going quiet, or suddenly needing a nap at ten in the morning, or asking the same question three times about what time the truck is coming. None of that is the furniture. It’s the day.

A few things help more than they sound like they should.

Give the parent one job that’s theirs alone, something small enough to finish but real enough to matter. Directing which box of kitchen things goes in the car instead of the truck, deciding which photo gets carried by hand, walking the movers through which pieces need extra care. A job with a clear finish gives a parent something to do with the morning besides watch it happen to them.

Protect one quiet space for as long as possible. If the move is happening in stages, keep one room untouched until last, a bedroom or a den, so there’s somewhere to sit that still looks like the house instead of a staging area. Watching every room empty out at once, all morning, is harder than watching it happen gradually.

Don’t rush the goodbye, and don’t skip it either. Some families walk a parent through the empty house at the very end, room by room, before locking the door for the last time. Others find that unbearable and skip straight from the last box to the car. Ask the parent which they’d rather do, and don’t assume the answer is the same as what worked for somebody else’s family. There isn’t a right way to leave a house you’ve lived in for decades. There’s only the way that doesn’t add more weight to a day that already has plenty.

And build in real breaks — not “we’ll stop if we have time,” but an actual lunch, sitting down, away from boxes, at a set time on the schedule. A parent who’s tired, hungry and surrounded by people moving fast is more likely to get overwhelmed than one who’s had a sandwich and twenty quiet minutes.

Pack last, unpack first

One of the more useful habits for moving day has nothing to do with the moving truck and everything to do with the first hour in the new place. What goes on the truck last comes off first, so think ahead about what needs to be in a parent’s hands within the first hour of arriving somewhere new, not buried under everything else.

A short list that tends to matter most: the bed, made up and ready, so there’s somewhere to lie down the first night without digging through boxes. A few familiar photos or small objects already out on a shelf or nightstand, not packed in a box marked “misc.” Any current medicines, which should never ride in the moving truck at all — they travel with the parent, in a bag they keep with them, the same rule Chapter 12 already set for sorting. A phone charger, a change of clothes, basic toiletries, and whatever single object a parent would ask for first if the rest of the boxes didn’t show up until tomorrow — a specific chair, a particular blanket, a clock that’s always sat on the same dresser.

Label a small set of boxes “open first” and keep them separate from the truck’s general load — in the car, if there’s room, or loaded last and unloaded first if there isn’t. The goal is a new place that feels at least a little familiar within the first hour, not a maze of identical boxes with no way to tell which one has the thing that actually matters tonight.

A run sheet for the day itself

Link the day’s run sheet to the move entry in Chapter 10’s plan.

A simple run sheet for the day itself, built the week before and printed out, not improvised that morning, might look something like this:

7:30 a.m. — Arrive at old house, confirm “open first” boxes are loaded last or set aside for the car.

8:00 a.m. — Movers arrive, walk the house with them one more time, confirm the inventory list against what’s actually there.

8:00 a.m.–12:00 p.m. — Loading. Parent has their one assigned job during this window — directing small items, checking a final room, whatever was agreed ahead of time.

12:00 p.m. — Lunch, sitting down, away from the truck. Non-negotiable, on the schedule the same as loading is.

1:00 p.m. — Final walkthrough of the old house, goodbye if the parent wants one.

1:30 p.m. — Truck departs. Confirm delivery address and timing with the driver one more time before it leaves the driveway.

2:30–4:00 p.m. — Arrival at new place. “Open first” boxes unloaded immediately: bed made, a few familiar objects out, medicines handed to the parent directly.

Get through the door before the truck

Add an entry appointment to that schedule. A delivery address doesn’t tell you who will unlock the apartment. Confirm the key handover with the actual contact, including a number that will be answered during the arrival window. If an elevator or loading entrance needs booking, get the building’s instructions before departure. Put those details beside arrival, not in somebody’s inbox.

For this sample afternoon, write: “2:15, designated arrival helper meets the building contact, collects keys and confirms the unit is accessible; call the parent companion with entry instructions.” Replace that helper label with a name. The person riding with your parent should know where they can go without standing beside a truck while someone searches for a manager.

Keep the car-held essentials with that companion. Don’t unload them onto the pavement to make room for another carton. At the new address, take your parent inside first, to the place you’ve agreed they can sit while furniture comes in. Ask whether they want to direct the familiar objects or leave that to you.

If the truck is delayed, separate tonight’s needs from the full delivery. Check what is actually available for eating, washing and sleeping. Tell your parent what you know, without inventing an arrival time. A blanket and toiletries won’t replace a missing bed. Use the delay arrangement confirmed with the mover and new home, or ask the appropriate contact about an alternative before promising one.

The useful update is “we can get inside, and here’s tonight’s arrangement,” not “everything should be fine.”

If a parent gets overwhelmed partway through

Even a well-planned day can run into a moment where a parent is visibly done — overwhelmed, tearful, shut down, or simply saying they want to stop. That’s not a failure of the plan. It’s a person reacting to a genuinely hard day exactly the way a hard day deserves to be reacted to. A pause is for ordinary distress. New confusion, chest pain, trouble breathing, a fall or injury, stroke signs, or immediate danger is not a moving-day feeling to manage; follow emergency instructions or get urgent medical help.

When that happens, the instinct is often to push through, because the truck is loading and the schedule says noon. There isn’t time to stop, or so it feels. Resist that instinct if you can. A fifteen-minute pause, somewhere quiet, with one person sitting with the parent and not talking about boxes, usually does more good than finishing on schedule. If one family member is calmer under pressure than the rest, or isn’t also trying to coordinate the movers, that’s who should sit with the parent in that moment. Not necessarily whoever happens to be free.

If the overwhelm runs deeper than a pause can fix, real distress rather than ordinary tiredness, it’s reasonable to slow the whole day down. Before moving day, ask the mover and the new home what a pause or later arrival changes — the price, loading cutoff, delivery window, and who must approve it — then put that contingency on the run sheet. This is also where having kept the day’s decisions to a minimum pays off. A day with nothing left to decide is a day that can pause and restart without anything falling apart, because the only thing happening is loading a truck, not making choices under pressure.

Watch, too, for the parent who insists they’re fine when they clearly aren’t. Some people manage a hard day by performing calm, and the performance can hold right up until it doesn’t. A sudden round of tears in the car. A silence that lasts through dinner. If you notice someone working hard to seem okay, a quiet check-in later in the day, away from the activity, often gets a more honest answer than asking in the middle of the loading. A steady face at ten in the morning doesn’t always mean a steady afternoon follows it.

What this day isn’t

Moving day is not the day to finish sorting a room that got skipped, divide an item siblings never resolved, or negotiate a repair the house sale didn’t settle. If any of that is still open when the truck arrives, it gets boxed and dealt with later. A garage, a storage unit, a sibling’s spare room will all hold a box longer than movers will hold a truck in the driveway while the family argues. A day this heavy doesn’t have room for decisions that should have been made the week before.

It’s also not the day to judge how the move is going. A parent who’s quiet, or short-tempered, or crying in the car on the way to the new place is not evidence the move was a mistake. It’s evidence that leaving a house is hard, which it is, for almost everyone, almost every time. Chapter 19 covers what settling in actually looks like over the weeks that follow, and it takes longer than one afternoon tells you it will. Moving day’s only real job is getting everyone and everything to the new address safely, with the first hour there feeling as familiar as a box of labeled essentials can make it feel.

The father who watched his furniture leave through the front door that morning still talks about those few hours as the hardest part of the whole move. He also says, now, that the thing that actually helped wasn’t the laminated schedule. It was his daughter sitting with him for fifteen minutes around eleven, not talking about the truck, just sitting. The schedule got the boxes where they needed to go. The fifteen minutes got him through the day, and it’s worth building that kind of fifteen minutes into the plan on purpose rather than hoping it happens by accident.

A run sheet with every box checked off and a truck that arrived on time is not, by itself, proof that the day went well. The day went well if the parent got through it feeling cared for rather than managed. Both things usually take the same amount of planning. They just don’t take the same kind of attention.

Chapter 18: Setting Up the New Home for Safety

In one composite move, a daughter furnished her mother’s apartment in a week — couch against the far wall, a rug under the coffee table for warmth, a floor lamp in the corner for reading. It looked finished. It looked, honestly, like a magazine spread for someone starting over. Six weeks later her mother caught her foot on the edge of that rug in the dark, reaching for the bathroom, and went down hard enough to need a trip to urgent care in this illustration. Nothing broke. It could have.

The apartment hadn’t failed. The decorating instinct had just outrun the safety instinct, and that’s an easy thing to do when you’re exhausted and trying to make a new place feel like home fast. A new home needs both things done at once, not one after the other.

Lighting first, before anything else gets arranged

One easy change people often overlook is better lighting. A hallway that seems fine during a daytime walkthrough can be dark at ten at night, when someone may be walking to the bathroom.

Put a light, or a switch within reach of the bed, on the path from the bedroom to the bathroom. Nightlights along that same route, plugged in low enough to light the floor rather than glare in the eyes. In rooms with dimmer or older fixtures, swap in brighter bulbs before move-in day rather than after someone’s already stumbled in a dim room. Test existing lights at night. For a new switch, fixture or wiring, ask building management or a qualified electrician rather than improvising. Walk the route a parent will actually walk at night, at night, before deciding the lighting is adequate.

Clearing the floor a parent will actually walk

Trip hazards are rarely dramatic. They’re the ordinary things that look fine in daylight and disappear underfoot in the dark or at the edge of someone’s vision. A loose area rug. An extension cord crossing a doorway. A stack of still-unpacked boxes left in a hallway because the garage filled up first. The fix for most of it isn’t complicated. It’s just easy to put off when there’s a whole apartment to set up and only so many hours in a day.

Walk every path a parent will actually use: bedroom to bathroom, bedroom to kitchen, front door to the nearest chair. Look at each one the way a tired person moving slowly would look at it, not the way someone unpacking boxes at full speed does. Remove throw and small area rugs from walking paths entirely; the National Institute on Aging’s room-by-room guidance advises against them, not just securing them. A nonskid bath mat on a wet bathroom surface is a different thing from an area rug in a night path, and it’s the one exception worth keeping. Tape or route cords along a wall instead of across an open floor. Keep furniture placement wide enough for a clear, unbroken path. Don’t let it become a maze around a side table or an ottoman someone liked the look of. Boxes belong in a spare room or garage, not stacked along the one hallway that gets used every day. This is the same practical logic Chapter 12’s room-by-room sorting used. The question is still where something goes, just now in the new place instead of the old one.

The CDC’s falls-prevention guidance for older adults lists this same ground-floor work alongside medical steps like reviewing medications and checking vision. Get rid of things you could trip over. Add grab bars inside and outside the tub or shower and next to the toilet. Put railings on both sides of stairs. Add more or brighter light throughout the home. It’s not a checklist unique to this book. It’s standard guidance, repeated here because most people don’t think of a move as the moment to act on it, even though a move is exactly when every room gets rearranged anyway.

What’s a project for a professional, not a weekend task

Grab bars, raised toilet seats bolted to the floor, handrails added to a short flight of steps — these belong on a different list than lighting and rugs. They need to go into a stud or be anchored properly to hold real weight under a real fall. A bar that pulls out of drywall the first time someone leans on it is worse than no bar at all, because it gave a false sense of security right up until it failed. This isn’t a Saturday-afternoon project with a cordless drill. It’s a job for an occupational therapist or a qualified home-safety installer who can assess where a parent actually needs support and install it to hold.

If a facility or complex already has grab bars and railings installed as part of its building, that’s a different situation. Confirm they’re there and placed where your parent needs them, rather than assuming every bathroom comes equipped the same way. For a private home or apartment, don’t guess at placement yourself. An occupational therapist evaluates how a specific person moves through a specific space and recommends fixed equipment accordingly. That’s worth more than a bar installed wherever seemed logical from the hardware store aisle.

The Eldercare Locator, which Chapter 10 already named for local referrals, is a reasonable place to start if a professional home-safety assessment is wanted and there’s no contact for one in the new area yet. Reach it through eldercare.acl.gov or 1-800-677-1116. A referral through a parent’s own doctor works just as well, if that relationship already exists in the new area or can travel with them from the old one.

A room-by-room pass before move-in day finishes

This doesn’t need to happen all in one sitting. It shouldn’t wait until everything feels unpacked and settled either. Better to check it early, while furniture is still being arranged and before anyone’s settled into a routine around a hazard nobody noticed. Give this pass its own line on the Chapter 10 plan, with a name and a date beside it.

Test the actual bedroom-to-bathroom route after dark. Use this checklist:

  • Bedroom: hazard — no light within reach of bed, or clutter on the floor path. Fix — add a lamp or nightlight; clear the path to the door. Fixed equipment, if needed, waits for a qualified installer after individualized assessment.
  • Bathroom: hazard — a sliding mat, dim lighting over sink or shower, or no grab bar where one’s needed. Fix — a nonskid bath mat; brighter bulbs; note grab-bar placement for the pending occupational therapist or installer rather than guessing yourself.
  • Kitchen: hazard — frequently used items stored above reach, requiring a step stool. Fix — move them to shelves within easy reach.
  • Walkways and stairs: hazard — loose rugs, trailing cords, a wobbly handrail, or dim lighting at the top or bottom of a flight. Fix — clear the floor, secure cords. If a handrail is loose or missing, keep your parent off those stairs; arrange another route and ask building management or a qualified installer to repair and check both rails before the stairs are used.
  • Exterior: hazard — uneven pavement or poor lighting between the parking spot and the front door. Fix — raise it with building management if that stretch is their responsibility.

None of this is a formal inspection, and it isn’t a substitute for one. A room can pass a daytime glance and still fail the test that matters, which is how it looks and feels to someone moving through it slowly, half-awake, at eleven at night.

Making the space recognizable, not just safe

Chapter 17 already covered getting a handful of recognizable objects unpacked first. The safety task here is narrower: confirm the parent-approved chair, bedside light, walking aid and route placement, with a clinician or occupational therapist if mobility is uncertain. Ask your parent which familiar pieces help this room feel like theirs; place them where they do not obstruct the walking route. Emotional adjustment to the new place belongs to Chapter 19, not here.

Arrange furniture, where it’s safe to do so, in something close to a familiar configuration — a favorite chair facing the television the way it always did, a side table in the same relative spot to that chair even if the room itself is a different shape. Preserve familiar furniture where a clear path permits; a few deliberate echoes of the old arrangement, placed where they don’t block a walking path, do real work toward making an unfamiliar room feel less like a stranger’s apartment.

Two more things worth five minutes each

Footwear gets overlooked in all of this, and it shouldn’t. Slippers that slide, socks on bare floor, shoes with worn-down treads: all of it raises the odds of exactly the kind of fall this whole chapter is trying to prevent. Keep supportive, nonskid footwear by the bed. Ask an occupational therapist where grab bars or other supports are needed too; shoes do not replace them.

The entry and exit points matter too, not just the interior. Check the path from the parking spot or curb to the front door for the same hazards you checked indoors: uneven pavement, a step without a handrail, poor lighting after dark. A beautifully safe apartment doesn’t help much if the walk from the car to the door is the actual risk. If the building or complex is responsible for that stretch, raise it with management directly rather than assuming someone else already has.

The handoff conversation with the landlord or facility

Independent of anything the family arranges itself, the building or facility already owns some of this safety picture, and it’s worth finding out exactly what before move-in day rather than assuming. A rented apartment, a 55+ community, and an assisted-living facility each carry a different mix of what management maintains and what the resident is responsible for, and that line isn’t always where a family guesses it is.

Ask management directly, in writing if possible, who is responsible for each of the following, and keep the written answer in the same folder Chapter 10 set up for move records:

  • Grab bars and handrails already installed in the bathroom and on any interior or exterior steps — confirm they exist, where exactly they’re placed, and whether they were professionally installed to hold real weight, rather than assuming a bar on the wall is anchored into something solid.
  • Who to call, and how quickly someone responds, if a grab bar loosens, a railing wobbles, or a light fixture stops working after move-in.
  • Whether smoke detectors and carbon monoxide detectors are already installed, whether management tests and replaces the batteries, or whether that falls to the resident.
  • Lighting in shared hallways, stairwells, parking areas, and building entrances — confirm it’s adequate and ask who to notify if a bulb burns out or a motion sensor stops working.
  • Snow and ice removal on shared walkways, in climates where that applies, and how quickly it’s typically handled after a storm.
  • Whether an emergency call system, pull cord, or pendant alert is included, how it’s tested, and what happens when it’s activated — who responds, and how fast.
  • Policy on space heaters, scatter rugs in common areas, or other items the building restricts for fire or fall-safety reasons; some facilities prohibit these outright, and it’s better to know before buying one.
  • Whether maintenance staff can access the apartment for a safety check or repair without extensive advance notice, in the event something needs attention quickly.

For a facility rather than a private rental, ask what the standard room setup includes for fall prevention. Ask whether staff can walk through the specific room with the family before or shortly after move-in. Confirm who would conduct the review and what it covers.

Get the answers to all of this in writing somewhere, even if it’s just a dated note of what a staff member told you on the phone. A verbal answer from a leasing agent at move-in has a way of becoming impossible to track down again by the time something actually goes wrong.

A short handoff checklist

Use this alongside the room-by-room pass above, not instead of it — the room-by-room pass covers what the family sets up; this covers what the building already owns:

  • Grab bars and handrails: confirmed present, placement checked, professionally installed — yes or no, and who to call if one fails.
  • Smoke and carbon monoxide detectors: confirmed working, battery responsibility identified.
  • Shared-area lighting (hallway, stairwell, entrance, parking): confirmed adequate, contact identified for an outage.
  • Snow and ice removal, where applicable: typical response time confirmed.
  • Emergency call system or pendant: included or not, tested, response process confirmed.
  • Building restrictions (space heaters, rugs, extension cords in common areas): confirmed and noted.
  • Maintenance access for a safety repair: typical response time confirmed.
  • Facility-specific walkthrough with occupational therapy or nursing staff: requested, scheduled, or declined.

Put a name and a date beside each line, the habit Chapter 10 already set for every task in this move. A building’s safety features are only as good as the family’s actual knowledge of which ones exist and who to call when one needs attention.

If you want a professional opinion on the whole space

Not every family needs or wants a formal home-safety assessment, and this book isn’t telling you that you do. But if a parent has already had a fall, has vision or balance concerns, or the new place has stairs or a layout that worries you, it’s reasonable to ask for one rather than guess your way through it alone. An occupational therapist can do a home visit and assess the space specifically, room by room, for that person’s actual needs — not a generic checklist, but an evaluation of how they move, reach, and balance in their own rooms. Ask the parent’s doctor or Eldercare Locator whether a local assessment or occupational-therapy referral is available; confirm cost and scheduling.

This is also, incidentally, a reasonable moment to raise anything that’s come up since the move started — a near-miss, a new unsteadiness, a complaint about dizziness getting up from a chair. None of that is something this book is equipped to evaluate. It’s something a doctor is, and raising it costs nothing but a phone call.

A move is disruptive enough on its own that it’s easy to write off a stumble or a dizzy spell as “just the stress of everything right now.” Sometimes that’s all it is. Sometimes it isn’t, and the only way to tell the difference is to say it out loud to someone qualified to ask follow-up questions, rather than deciding privately that it’s nothing. A parent who downplays a near-fall to avoid worrying anyone is doing the opposite of what actually helps them. The CDC’s own guidance puts a doctor conversation first, ahead of any home modification, for exactly this reason: a fall or a close call can be a sign of something medical worth catching early, not just a loose rug worth tightening.

The mother in this composite healed up fine from the fall, and the rug came up the next morning, leaving that stretch of floor bare and clear. What stuck was how much of the apartment had been arranged for how it looked before anyone walked it at night, the way she actually would. The couch was in the right place. The lamp worked. Nobody had checked the floor.

Walk the new place once, slowly, in the evening, before you call it finished. That one walk will tell you more than any amount of arranging furniture in good daylight ever will, and it costs nothing but the 20 minutes it takes to do it.

Chapter 19: Settling In and Siblings Going Forward

For two weeks after Dad moved into independent living, he ate supper alone. He didn’t want me making introductions. The dining room was full enough. He just hadn’t found his way into anybody’s routine. Then a staff member learned he’d worked in a textile mill and paired him with another former mill man. They had something easy to start with: shifts, machines, the small complaints of a long workday. Earl began sitting with him.

The new address was right. The first two weeks still felt lonely.

That’s the part a truck schedule can’t solve. Your parent may know why the move happened and still miss the ordinary shape of the old life: which neighbor dropped by, where the mail landed, how supper began. Don’t read a quiet first week as a verdict on the home. Don’t dismiss it, either. Settling in deserves its own plan, with your parent in the driver’s seat wherever they can be.

The first days are information, not a verdict

A move rearranges more than furniture. Your parent has to learn which door to use, where to ask for help, when things happen, and which familiar habits still fit. In a smaller home, that may mean working out a new route to the grocery store or finding a regular place to have coffee. In a community, it may mean recognizing a few faces and learning which activities are actually enjoyable. A brochure’s promise of connection is not the same as having someone to sit with on Tuesday.

There is no universal settling-in timetable. One person may want company on the first evening; another may want the phone left alone until morning. The useful expectation is that adjustment may take weeks rather than days, and that the first few days don’t tell you everything. That is not a reason to ignore a parent’s concerns or wait through a problem that needs attention. It’s permission to ask, observe, and make a small adjustment before declaring success or failure.

Start with the parent’s own account. Ask one open question, then give them time to answer. “What’s been easier than you expected?” or “What part of the day feels awkward so far?” is better than a string of questions designed to prove the move was right. If the answer is “I don’t know,” try again later, or offer two specific choices: “Would you rather have lunch here or take a drive to the cafe?” Keep the choice genuine. A question with only one acceptable answer is a sales pitch in a cardigan.

Listen for practical friction as well as emotion. Maybe a bus schedule is hard to read, a meal time conflicts with a familiar routine, or a favorite activity isn’t available on the days your parent can get there. Ask what they would like to change. Write down the concrete request in their words, with their permission, and identify who can answer it. Don’t turn a complaint into a character judgment: “The dining room is too loud” is information, not proof that your parent refuses to try.

If your parent reports a new or worsening health problem, a fall, severe distress, or a safety concern, contact the appropriate health professional or responsible staff promptly. A move is not an explanation for every change. For ordinary loneliness or frustration, offer attention and choices; for a medical or immediate safety concern, get qualified help rather than trying to interpret it as an adjustment phase.

Ask about welcome before moving day

If the next home is a community or facility, ask what actually happens after a resident arrives. Some have a welcome contact, orientation, introductions or optional activities; others may not, or may offer them differently. Using the Chapter 11 tour answer about activities, ask the administrator or resident-services contact how the agreed welcome step gets from the brochure to your parent’s door. If your parent wants you included, confirm what information staff may share and how to give them permission to speak with you. Don’t assume that being an adult child automatically puts you on every update.

A few questions make the conversation useful:

  • Is there an orientation or welcome program, and what does it include?
  • Who will actually follow up with my parent, and how soon after arrival?
  • What is that person’s name and contact method, and whom can my parent contact if the agreed welcome step never happens?
  • How do residents get to activities or shared spaces, and are there costs or sign-ups?
